meta.title: How to Calculate RMD: Balance, IRS Factor and Remaining Withdrawal
meta.heading: How to Calculate RMD: Balance, IRS Factor and Remaining Withdrawal
meta.description: Calculate an owner-account RMD from the prior December 31 balance and IRS factor. Compare ages, credited distributions and deadlines with reproducible examples.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate RMD: Balance, IRS Factor and Remaining Withdrawal
meta.cardIntro: Calculate an owner-account RMD from the prior December 31 balance and IRS factor. Compare ages, credited distributions and deadlines with reproducible examples.

rmd.intro: Calculate an owner-account required minimum distribution by dividing the prior December 31 balance by the applicable IRS distribution period for your age in the distribution year. Confirm that an RMD applies and that you selected the right table before doing the division. Inherited accounts have different rules and are outside this calculator’s owner-account model.
rmd.answer: For an owner turning 75 in 2026 using the Uniform Lifetime Table, the factor is 24.6. A $500,000 balance on December 31, 2025 produces a gross 2026 RMD of $20,325.20 rounded to cents. If $10,000 of eligible gross distributions is already credited to that 2026 RMD, the remaining modeled requirement is $10,325.20.

sections.title: Use the correct year-end balance and birthday age
paragraphs: A 2026 RMD uses the December 31, 2025 balance, not today’s value after this year’s market changes. Use the age you reach by the end of 2026, even if the birthday has not yet occurred when you calculate. The factor and the balance refer to different dates for a reason: the previous year-end establishes the calculation base.

Confirm account type and any necessary adjustments with the custodian. Do not put a Roth IRA owner balance into this model; Roth IRA owners have no lifetime RMD. Designated Roth plan accounts also have no owner lifetime RMD for 2024 onward. Inherited-account requirements and still-working employer-plan exceptions need separate review.

sections.title: Choose the applicable IRS distribution table
paragraphs: The examples use Table III, the Uniform Lifetime Table in IRS Publication 590-B: 26.5 at age 73, 24.6 at age 75 and 20.2 at age 80. They are three separate owners in 2026 with identical prior year-end balances. They are not a projection claiming that one account remains at $500,000 while its owner ages.

The calculator can use Table II when the sole beneficiary is a spouse more than ten years younger, using both spouses’ ages. That condition is more specific than simply being married. If the spouse is not the sole beneficiary or the age difference does not meet the rule, do not select the younger-spouse option merely to reduce a result.
sections.formula: Gross annual RMD = eligible previous December 31 balance / applicable IRS distribution period

sections.title: Subtract eligible gross distributions only once
paragraphs: The annual requirement and remaining requirement are separate outputs. Enter gross distributions credited to the selected year’s RMD before withholding. A net bank deposit can be smaller than the gross amount already distributed from the retirement account. Reconcile the number with custodian records rather than comparing only what arrived in checking.

Do not include a delayed prior-year first RMD as credit toward the current year’s requirement. Excess distributions do not become a future-year RMD credit. In our age-75 case, the $10,000 credited amount reduces the remaining requirement but does not change the original $20,325.20 annual calculation.
sections.formula: Remaining selected-year RMD = max(0, annual RMD − eligible gross distributions credited to that year)

sections.title: A first-year deadline can create two distributions in one calendar year
paragraphs: For an IRA owner reaching 73 in 2026 under the applicable rule, the first distribution year is 2026. The first RMD can generally be delayed until April 1, 2027; the 2027 RMD still has its own December 31, 2027 deadline. Delaying therefore can place two RMDs in 2027. Their calculation balances and distribution years remain separate.

Under the birth-year rules used here, owners born from 1951 through 1959 start at 73, while those born in 1960 or later start at 75. Earlier cohorts and employer-plan exceptions require context. The calculator’s selected year does not automatically decide the tax consequence of a delay or establish that a workplace-plan exception applies. The current regulation leaves the paragraph for the 1959 cohort reserved; confirm applicable guidance with the plan or custodian rather than treating this model’s birth-year setting as a legal determination.

sections.title: Understand the optional projection and monthly budgeting number
paragraphs: The monthly budgeting equivalent is the annual RMD divided by twelve. It is not an IRS rule requiring twelve equal payments. The age-75 example gives roughly $1,693.77 per month as a budgeting figure while the annual requirement remains the operative amount.

For a projection, the model applies the entered constant return to the opening balance and then withdraws at year-end. First-year modeled withdrawal is the greater of the RMD and credited distributions, rather than their sum. Future rows use changing age factors and modeled closing balances. Actual withdrawal timing, extra distributions and variable returns can change future balances, so the first-year statutory arithmetic and multi-year projection should not be interpreted as equally certain.

rmd.chartAlt: Annual owner RMDs for separate people aged 73, 75 and 80 with the same $500,000 prior December 31 balance.
rmd.chartCaption: Table III factors are 26.5, 24.6 and 20.2. Age and factor change across the chart; all three prior year-end balances are $500,000.

questions.question: What balance do I use to calculate my 2026 RMD?
questions.answer: Generally use the eligible account balance on December 31, 2025, with any required adjustments confirmed by the custodian. A current balance after market moves is not the ordinary calculation base.

questions.question: Which age determines the RMD factor?
questions.answer: Use the age you reach by the end of the distribution year. Table II requires both spouses’ ages when its younger sole-beneficiary spouse conditions apply.

questions.question: Does withholding count toward the amount withdrawn?
questions.answer: Use the gross eligible distribution credited by the custodian, including amounts withheld for tax. The net deposit into your bank account is not necessarily the RMD credit.

questions.question: Can I carry an excess withdrawal forward to next year?
questions.answer: No. Taking more than one year’s RMD does not create credit against a later year’s requirement. The next calculation uses its own balance, age and rules.

questions.question: Can I calculate an inherited IRA RMD with this tool?
questions.answer: No. This model is for supported owner accounts. Beneficiary status, inheritance date, owner death and other conditions affect inherited-account rules; use appropriate IRS guidance and custodian advice.

questions.question: Does dividing the RMD by twelve create a monthly deadline?
questions.answer: No. It is a budgeting equivalent. Confirm the annual deadline and your custodian’s processing schedule; the tool does not mandate monthly distributions.

limitations: Owner-account illustration using verified post-2021 tables; no inherited-account, still-working exception or individualized deadline determination.
Gross RMD is not take-home income. Withholding, marginal tax brackets and Medicare-related effects are not calculated.
Future returns and year-end withdrawal timing are projection assumptions, not IRS-mandated account performance.

meta.title: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.heading: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.description: Calculate two-tier 401(k) matching, distinguish match rate from salary band, and understand contribution limits, payroll timing, true-ups and vesting.
meta.breadcrumb: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.cardIntro: Calculate two-tier 401(k) matching, distinguish match rate from salary band, and understand contribution limits, payroll timing, true-ups and vesting.

matching.intro: A 401(k) employer match adds money under your employer’s plan formula when you make qualifying contributions. The match rate tells you how much the employer adds per eligible dollar. The contribution band tells you how much of your pay is eligible for that rate. Read both numbers together; a 50% match does not usually mean the employer deposits half of your annual salary.
matching.answer: At $80,000 annual salary, a plan matching 100% of the first 3% contributed plus 50% of the next 2% requires a $4,000 employee contribution to capture the full modeled match. The employer contributes $3,200, or 4% of salary. The combined $7,200 contribution is not the same as contributing only 4% yourself.

sections.title: Translate the match sentence into contribution bands
paragraphs: Break the formula into separate slices. The first 3% of $80,000 is $2,400, matched dollar for dollar. The next 2% is $1,600, matched at 50% for another $800. Adding the two employer amounts gives $3,200. Employee contributions across both bands total $4,000, or 5% of salary.

In the calculator’s second tier, enter the additional band, not the cumulative threshold. For “100% on the first 3%, then 50% through 5%,” the additional second band is 2%, not 5%. A wrong interpretation would model an 8% combined band and overstate the employee contribution needed.
sections.formula: Employer match = eligible first-band employee dollars × first rate + eligible additional-band dollars × second rate

sections.title: Same salary, three matching policies
paragraphs: Our chart holds salary at $80,000 and assumes the employee contributes enough to earn the full modeled match. The two-tier example produces $3,200. A 50% match on the first 6% needs $4,800 employee dollars and produces $2,400 employer dollars. A 100% match on the first 6% also needs $4,800 but produces $4,800.

These controlled hypothetical policies demonstrate why headline match percentages are insufficient for comparing benefits. They are not a survey of typical employers. Compare eligibility, vesting, eligible compensation, contribution timing and other benefits before deciding which employment package is better.

sections.title: Employee deferrals and employer additions have different limits
paragraphs: For 2026, the basic employee elective-deferral limit is $24,500. Eligible participants age 50 or older may have an $8,000 catch-up, with the higher $11,250 catch-up applying at ages 60 through 63 if permitted. These are limits, not automatic entitlements to employer matching. Use calendar-year-end age and check plan eligibility.

The model uses the 2026 $360,000 eligible-compensation cap and $72,000 annual-additions cap excluding employee catch-up. Employer matching does not consume the employee elective-deferral limit, but combined additions have their own constraints. Other plans, prior contributions and plan restrictions can require adjustments outside this simplified full-year model.

In the high-salary case, $400,000 salary does not make all pay match-eligible: compensation is capped at $360,000. A 100% match on the first 10% would require $36,000 employee contributions. A 35-year-old’s $24,500 deferral limit prevents that under our assumptions, so the tool reports a partial match and explicitly labels full matching unattainable.

sections.title: Why reaching the limit early can change the match
paragraphs: The Maximize Employer Match mode assumes equal pay, a constant contribution percentage, per-pay-period matching and no annual true-up. The upper steady rate spreads the age-based employee limit over annual salary. If contributions stop before year-end, later pay periods may have no employee deferral to match.

Some plans reconcile matching annually through a true-up; others do not, and conditions can vary. Bonuses, pay changes, midyear enrollment and prior year-to-date contributions also change the payroll problem. Ask the administrator how your actual plan treats them. The calculator’s steady-rate window is not a personalized payroll election.

sections.title: A credited match is different from money you are entitled to keep
paragraphs: Employee contributions and their earnings are fully vested, while employer contributions may be subject to a vesting schedule depending on plan design. The calculator reports modeled employer deposits without applying a vesting haircut. A $3,200 match is therefore not a guarantee that a departing employee keeps all $3,200.

Read the summary plan description for match formula, eligible pay, vesting, timing and true-up provisions. For a long-term projection, use the tool’s separate projection mode and review its contribution timing and fixed-year limits. A yearly matching calculation alone says nothing about future investment returns, tax treatment at withdrawal or how long savings will last.

matching.chartAlt: Annual employer matching dollars under three hypothetical policies at the same $80,000 salary with sufficient employee contributions.
matching.chartCaption: Employee contributions required are $4,000, $4,800 and $4,800 respectively. The separate high-salary case tests a binding employee limit.

questions.question: What does a 50% 401(k) match up to 6% mean?
questions.answer: Under that formula, each qualifying employee dollar receives 50 cents from the employer, up to employee contributions equal to 6% of eligible pay. At $80,000, $4,800 employee contributions can earn $2,400 employer contributions before other applicable restrictions.

questions.question: Does my employer match count toward the $24,500 employee limit?
questions.answer: Employer matching does not use the 2026 employee elective-deferral limit. Combined employee and employer annual additions have a separate limit, and catch-up contributions have separate treatment.

questions.question: How do I enter a two-tier matching formula?
questions.answer: Enter the first band and match rate, then the additional second band and its rate. A formula running from 3% through 5% has a 2% second band, not 5%.

questions.question: Should I contribute the annual maximum as early as possible?
questions.answer: That depends on the plan’s matching timing and true-up provisions. With per-pay-period matching and no true-up, stopping deferrals early may lose later matching opportunities. This mode illustrates a steady full-year rate rather than optimizing every payroll.

questions.question: Is the employer match immediately vested?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. The plan’s vesting rules govern ownership of employer contributions. This calculator reports the modeled deposit and does not calculate a forfeiture at departure.

questions.question: Can this mode calculate a midyear payroll change?
questions.answer: Not directly. It assumes full-year employment, equal pay, constant contributions and no prior year-to-date deferrals. Use your actual payroll and plan information for a midyear election.

limitations: Matching rules are hypothetical inputs. This guide does not assert that a particular employer offers them or that every plan permits catch-up contributions.
The steady-rate model excludes bonuses, unequal pay, prior contributions, annual true-ups and vesting adjustments.
2026 contribution limits are versioned inputs, not a forecast of later years or a guarantee that payroll accepts the displayed rate.

meta.title: How to Calculate Net Operating Income for a Rental Property
meta.heading: How to Calculate Net Operating Income for a Rental Property
meta.description: Calculate property NOI from rent, vacancy and operating expenses. Includes monthly and annual examples, spreadsheet formulas and the difference from financed cash flow.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Net Operating Income for a Rental Property
meta.cardIntro: Calculate property NOI from rent, vacancy and operating expenses. Includes monthly and annual examples, spreadsheet formulas and the difference from financed cash flow.

noi.intro: Property net operating income, or NOI, is effective operating income less ordinary property operating expenses. It measures the property before its financing structure, capital replacements and the owner’s income tax. Start with a consistent reporting period, reconcile the income actually expected, and then subtract the appropriate costs. Do not substitute a tax-return net-income figure without checking what it includes.
noi.answer: In our hypothetical example, $4,000 scheduled monthly rent loses 5% to vacancy and collection loss. Add $100 other monthly income to get $3,900 effective income. Subtract $1,250 operating expenses: monthly NOI is $2,650 and annual NOI is $31,800. Mortgage payments, capital reserves and owner income tax are excluded.

sections.title: Start with effective income, not the advertised rent
paragraphs: Scheduled rent is the potential rent before the entered vacancy and collection allowance. At $4,000 per month and 5% loss, the allowance is $200. Adding $100 from an illustrative ancillary income source produces $3,900 effective operating income. The allowance applies only to scheduled rent in this model; other income should already reflect its own expected losses.

If your records already show collected rent after vacancy, subtracting another allowance can double-count the same loss. Reconstruct potential rent or choose inputs that consistently describe actual collected income. Keep refundable deposits, loan proceeds and an anticipated sale out of recurring property operating income. These are different cash movements, not additional rent.
sections.formula: Effective income = scheduled rent × (1 − vacancy and collection-loss rate) + other operating income

sections.title: Choose operating expenses and keep financing separate
paragraphs: The base monthly operating costs are $400 property tax, $150 insurance, $250 routine repairs, $300 management, $100 owner-paid utilities and $50 other operating expenses. HOA is zero here. Their $1,250 sum includes ordinary costs of running this hypothetical property. The management entry is a dollar amount in the NOI Calculator, not a percentage.

This model excludes debt principal and interest, depreciation, major capital improvements, replacement reserves and the owner’s income tax. Property tax is an operating cost; the owner’s income tax is a separate concept. Lenders or appraisers may use adjusted NOI conventions, including different reserve treatments, so reconcile definitions before comparing their figure with this worksheet.

sections.title: Calculate NOI in one consistent period
paragraphs: For monthly entries, subtract monthly operating expenses from monthly effective income, then multiply by twelve. For annual entries, do the subtraction once with annual amounts. The annualized result is not a forecast of seasonal rent collections; it simply puts all entered amounts on the same reporting basis.

Switching the reporting-period selector reinterprets the values already entered. It does not multiply the form fields by twelve. Our annual-entry case therefore supplies $48,000 rent, $1,200 other income and $15,000 total expenses explicitly. It reconciles to the same $31,800 annual NOI as the monthly case.
sections.formula: NOI = effective operating income − operating expenses; annual NOI = monthly NOI × 12 when monthly inputs are used

sections.title: What changing vacancy and maintenance does to NOI
paragraphs: The chart holds scheduled rent, other income and operating expenses constant while changing rent loss from 5% to 20% and 100%. Annual NOI moves from $31,800 to $24,600 and then −$13,800. At 100% rent loss, the separately entered $100 monthly other income remains; this is not an assumption that all income disappears.

A separate case raises routine repair spending from $250 to $1,000 per month. Annual NOI falls by $9,000 to $22,800. These are controlled illustrations, not estimated vacancy rates or repair budgets for a real address. Some actual operating costs respond to occupancy, while these scenarios deliberately hold their entered dollar amounts fixed.

sections.title: Build a small NOI spreadsheet and reconcile the result
paragraphs: With the base monthly amounts, a spreadsheet check is =4000*(1-5%)+100-SUM(400,150,250,300,100,0,50). It returns $2,650 monthly NOI; multiply that cell by twelve for $31,800 annually. Keep scheduled rent, loss allowance and each expense on separate rows so you can audit changes.

NOI is an input to other decisions, not their final answer. Divide annual NOI by a consistently chosen price or value for cap rate. Subtract debt service to move toward cash flow after financing, then consider separate capital spending, reserves and taxes. IRS rental tax reporting may treat interest and depreciation differently from this operating-income analysis; the two worksheets serve different purposes.

noi.chartAlt: Annual NOI at five, twenty and one hundred percent rent loss with other income and operating expenses held fixed.
noi.chartCaption: Each charted case starts with $4,000 scheduled monthly rent, $100 other income and $1,250 monthly operating costs. Other income is not reduced by the rent-loss input.

questions.question: What is net operating income in real estate?
questions.answer: It is a property operating measure: effective operating income less ordinary operating expenses under a defined convention. This worksheet calculates it before debt service, capital costs and owner income tax.

questions.question: Does NOI include mortgage payments?
questions.answer: No. Mortgage principal and interest are financing cash flows in this model. Subtract debt service separately when estimating the owner’s cash flow.

questions.question: Does NOI include property tax and insurance?
questions.answer: Yes, ordinary property tax and property insurance are included as operating costs here. That does not mean the owner’s personal income tax is included.

questions.question: Is NOI the same as net income?
questions.answer: No. Accounting or taxable net income can include financing, depreciation and other adjustments excluded from this property NOI convention. Reconcile the components rather than assuming the labels are interchangeable.

questions.question: Can net operating income be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. When effective income is below operating costs, this tool retains the operating loss. It does not replace negative NOI with zero.

questions.question: How do I calculate annual NOI from monthly rent?
questions.answer: Use monthly rent, other income and operating expenses consistently, calculate monthly NOI and multiply by twelve. Do not annualize rent while leaving expenses monthly.

questions.question: Does changing the period selector convert my inputs?
questions.answer: No. It changes how the same entered amounts are interpreted. Enter converted annual dollar amounts yourself when changing from monthly to annual reporting.

limitations: This is a before-financing, before-capital-cost NOI convention; lender and appraisal adjustments can differ.
Vacancy applies only to scheduled rent; management is a dollar entry. Fixed operating costs do not automatically fall when rent is lost.
Examples are hypothetical operating scenarios, not market data, tax advice or appraisals.

meta.title: How to Calculate Cap Rate: Formula, NOI and Property Value
meta.heading: How to Calculate Cap Rate: Formula, NOI and Property Value
meta.description: Calculate cap rate from annual NOI and property value. Compare prices, estimate value at a target rate, and understand good cap rates, mortgage exclusions and ROI differences.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Cap Rate: Formula, NOI and Property Value
meta.cardIntro: Calculate cap rate from annual NOI and property value. Compare prices, estimate value at a target rate, and understand good cap rates, mortgage exclusions and ROI differences.

cap.intro: Calculate capitalization rate by dividing annual property NOI by the relevant property price or market value, then multiply by 100. It is an unlevered operating-income ratio, so mortgage payments are excluded. The usefulness of the result depends on consistent income assumptions and a denominator that answers the question you actually want to ask.
cap.answer: A property with $18,000 annual NOI and a $300,000 price has a 6% cap rate: 18,000 / 300,000 × 100. With the same NOI, a $360,000 value produces 5%, while a $240,000 value produces 7.5%. These are controlled price scenarios, not market valuations or recommended target rates.

sections.title: Use annual NOI in the cap rate formula
paragraphs: NOI starts with effective rental and other operating income, then subtracts ordinary property operating expenses. In this calculator it excludes mortgage payments, depreciation, capital improvements, replacement reserves and owner income tax. Use the separate NOI worksheet if the amount has not yet been reconciled.

Enter annual NOI, not monthly rent or the owner’s cash flow after loan payments. A monthly $1,500 NOI is $18,000 annually; putting $1,500 into the annual field understates the numerator by a factor of twelve. Gross rent is also the wrong substitute because it omits operating costs and vacancy.
sections.formula: Cap rate (%) = annual NOI / property price or market value × 100

sections.title: Choose purchase price or current market value deliberately
paragraphs: A purchase-price calculation uses the proposed or historical price to describe income relative to that amount. A current-value calculation uses the chosen valuation date’s market value. Those can produce different ratios for the same property. Your down payment is neither denominator; using it turns the ratio into a different and incomplete leverage calculation.

In the chart, $18,000 annual NOI stays unchanged while entered value moves from $300,000 to $360,000 and $240,000. The cap rate changes even though operating income does not. A higher quoted cap rate can therefore come from a lower price, a more optimistic NOI or both. Investigate the assumptions rather than comparing percentages alone.

sections.title: Calculate cap rate from a rental worksheet
paragraphs: Our worksheet case uses $4,000 scheduled monthly rent, 5% rent loss, $100 other monthly income and $1,250 monthly operating costs. Annual NOI is $31,800. At an entered $500,000 value, cap rate is 6.36%. This is a separate worksheet example, not another price-only variation of the $18,000 NOI cases.

The worksheet’s management cost is an entered dollar amount. Other tools on this site use a percentage of effective income, so translating a scenario between tools requires translating that field too. Select monthly or annual reporting consistently; the period selector reinterprets the entries instead of converting dollar amounts automatically.

sections.title: Estimate a value at a target rate without treating it as an appraisal
paragraphs: Rearranging the formula gives an indicated value equal to positive annual NOI divided by the target cap rate as a decimal. At $18,000 NOI and a chosen 6% target, the indicated value is $300,000. Changing the current entered property price does not change that indicated value when NOI and the target stay fixed.

For the worksheet’s $31,800 NOI, a 6% target indicates $530,000. That is a mathematical scenario, not a recommendation to offer $530,000. The target rate must be justified with compatible local comparables and an appropriate income basis. Zero or negative NOI cannot imply a meaningful positive value through this simple positive-rate capitalization method.
sections.formula: Indicated value at target rate = positive annual NOI / (target cap rate / 100)

sections.title: What is a good cap rate, and is a higher one better?
paragraphs: There is no universal good cap rate. Property type, location, lease quality, vacancy, repair needs, growth expectations and the income convention affect comparisons. A higher number is not automatic evidence of a safer or better deal; it can accompany risks or costs not captured by a headline NOI figure.

Cap rate is not total ROI, a mortgage-adjusted return or a guarantee of annual distributions. It omits appreciation, sale costs, financing and other cash flows. For cash remaining after debt service relative to invested cash, use cash-on-cash return and a complete cash budget. Our existing comparison glossary explains that distinction without creating another competing calculator page.

sections.title: Check the calculation in Excel or Google Sheets
paragraphs: For the base case, =18000/300000 gives 0.06; format the cell as a percentage to display 6%. Alternatively multiply by 100 and keep the cell numeric. Do not multiply by 100 and also apply percentage formatting, which would display 600%.

For indicated value, use =18000/6%. Keep income basis visible alongside the calculation: trailing actual results and forward stabilized assumptions can answer different questions. A scenario with −$6,000 annual NOI and $300,000 value has a signed −2% cap rate here, while the indicated positive value is intentionally reported as not meaningful.

cap.chartAlt: Cap rates of six, five and seven point five percent at three property values with the same $18,000 annual NOI.
cap.chartCaption: Only property value changes in the three charted cases. The table separately checks a rental worksheet, zero NOI and an operating loss.

questions.question: How do you calculate cap rate?
questions.answer: Divide annual property NOI by the relevant price or market value, then multiply by 100. For $18,000 annual NOI and $300,000 value, the result is 6%.

questions.question: Does cap rate include mortgage payments?
questions.answer: No. This is a before-financing ratio. Financing changes owner cash flow and invested cash, which should be examined separately.

questions.question: Is a higher cap rate always better?
questions.answer: No. A higher figure may reflect a lower price, higher risk or different income assumptions. Compare property condition, leases, vacancy, market evidence and a consistent NOI definition.

questions.question: Can I use monthly NOI to calculate cap rate?
questions.answer: Annualize it first. A $1,500 monthly NOI becomes $18,000 annually before dividing by value. This tool’s known-NOI mode expects annual dollars.

questions.question: Can cap rate be zero or negative?
questions.answer: Yes. The calculator displays zero or a signed negative ratio. It does not show a meaningful positive indicated value at a positive target rate when NOI is nonpositive.

questions.question: Is cap rate the same as cash-on-cash return?
questions.answer: No. Cap rate divides before-financing NOI by property value. Cash-on-cash uses a defined cash flow after financing divided by actual cash invested. Read the linked comparison for the full distinction.

questions.question: Can I estimate property value using cap rate?
questions.answer: For positive NOI, divide annual NOI by a justified target rate in decimal form. The result is an income-capitalization scenario, not a verified appraisal.

limitations: No current comparable-sales data, location-specific cap-rate recommendation or appraisal is supplied.
Income and value must use compatible dates, reporting periods and operating-cost conventions.
Signed operating losses are retained; positive-value capitalization is withheld for nonpositive NOI.

meta.title: How to Estimate Rental Property Cash Flow: A Worked Budget
meta.heading: How to Estimate Rental Property Cash Flow: A Worked Budget
meta.description: Estimate rental cash flow after vacancy, operating costs and debt service. Compare five scenarios, negative cash flow and reserve adjustments with a reproducible worksheet.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Estimate Rental Property Cash Flow: A Worked Budget
meta.cardIntro: Estimate rental cash flow after vacancy, operating costs and debt service. Compare five scenarios, negative cash flow and reserve adjustments with a reproducible worksheet.

rental.intro: Estimate rental property cash flow by moving from potential rent to effective income, subtracting ordinary operating costs, and then subtracting loan principal and interest. That produces a before-tax, before-separate-capital-reserve cash figure under this model. Include the remaining capital spending and tax obligations in your own liquidity budget before treating it as spendable income.
rental.answer: Our illustrative $300,000 rental earns $18,120 first-year NOI. A $225,000, 30-year loan at 6% requires $16,187.86 of first-year principal and interest, leaving $1,932.14 modeled annual cash flow, or a $161.01 monthly average. A separate $200 monthly capital reserve would turn that average budget into approximately −$38.99 before income tax.

sections.title: Build the income and operating-expense budget first
paragraphs: Start with $2,500 scheduled monthly rent and a 5% vacancy and collection allowance. With no other income in this example, effective annual income is $28,500. Management at 8% of effective income costs $2,280. Annual property tax of $3,600, insurance of $1,500 and routine maintenance of $3,000 add another $8,100.

Total first-year operating expenses are therefore $10,380, leaving $18,120 NOI. Management in the Rental Property Calculator is a percentage of collected rent plus other income. This differs from the separate NOI Calculator’s management-dollar field; translate the amount when moving the same property between tools.
sections.formula: Effective annual income = monthly rent × 12 × (1 − vacancy rate) + other monthly income × 12

sections.title: Subtract full debt service, not interest alone
paragraphs: A 25% down payment on $300,000 leaves a $225,000 loan. At a 6% nominal annual rate, monthly rate is 0.06 / 12 and term is 360 months. The resulting scheduled principal-and-interest payment is approximately $1,348.99 monthly. Keeping internal precision gives $16,187.86 of payments in the first year.

Subtract the entire payment for cash-flow purposes. Principal reduction builds equity, but the cash still leaves your account. Subtracting only interest overstates cash available for expenses. The initial cash investment here is $75,000 down payment plus $6,000 purchase closing costs and $10,000 initial repairs: $91,000 before any separately budgeted reserve.
sections.formula: First-year modeled cash flow = effective annual income − operating expenses − actual first-year principal and interest payments

sections.title: Stress-test vacancy, borrowing cost and rent
paragraphs: The chart changes one input from the base financed property in each stress case. Raising rent loss from 5% to 15% reduces annual cash flow to −$827.86. Raising the loan rate to 8%, with base rent loss retained, produces −$1,691.64. Reducing monthly scheduled rent to $2,000 produces −$3,311.86 at the original 6% loan rate.

These are hypothetical sensitivities, not market forecasts. The cash-purchase comparison removes debt service and raises initial invested cash from $91,000 to $316,000. Its $18,120 annual cash flow is larger, but comparing dollar cash flow alone ignores that extra capital. Cap rate remains tied to the property’s operating income and value rather than the financing choice.

sections.title: Add capital reserves and distinguish the monthly average
paragraphs: Routine maintenance is already included in the model’s operating expenses. A separately planned capital replacement reserve for a future roof or HVAC replacement is different. In the base case, annual flow of $1,932.14 minus $2,400 of planned annual capital reserve leaves about −$467.86, or −$38.99 monthly on average, before income tax.

That reserve adjustment is explained outside the Rental Property Calculator because it does not have a dedicated reserve cash-flow field. Putting the reserve into ordinary operating expenses changes the tool’s NOI and cap rate as well. Use the Cash-on-Cash Return Calculator’s disclosed reserve treatment when you need a separate reserve-aware comparison.

Annual cash flow divided by twelve is an average, not a promise that every month is positive. A vacancy month, insurance bill or repair can create a cash shortfall even when the annual total is positive. Maintain a separate timing budget for lumpy bills and access to cash; the first-year average does not solve liquidity risk.

sections.title: Positive operating cash flow does not guarantee a profitable investment
paragraphs: All checked scenarios use a one-year holding period, zero growth and zero appreciation to isolate first-year mechanics. The full tool can project annual rent and expense growth, loan balances and an eventual sale. Those future values are assumptions. A sale at the end of year one is included in the full investment-return model but is not included in the recurring first-year cash-flow figure.

For example, the base case has $1,932.14 positive recurring annual cash flow, yet a hypothetical sale at the unchanged $300,000 price with 6% selling costs produces an overall investment loss after initial outlays. Sale proceeds, equity, recurring cash and total profit must remain separate. Depreciation deductions, income taxes and capital-gains tax are outside this projection.

sections.title: Reproduce the first-year estimate in a spreadsheet
paragraphs: First calculate effective income with =2500*12*(1-5%). Then calculate operating costs with =3600+1500+3000+28500*8%. For scheduled debt service, =-PMT(6%/12,30*12,225000)*12 returns the first-year payment total for this full-year loan example. Subtract costs and debt service from income.

Keep vacancy, management, loan rate and reserve budget in separate cells. Test one change at a time before combining several adverse assumptions. The CSV below provides complete calculator inputs and reference metrics, while each preset link restores the same case in the existing tool.

rental.chartAlt: Monthly average cash flow under base financing, higher vacancy, higher loan rate, lower rent and a cash purchase.
rental.chartCaption: Cash flow is first-year income less operating costs and debt service, divided by twelve. Separate capital reserves and owner taxes are excluded from the chart.

questions.question: How do I estimate rental property cash flow?
questions.answer: Estimate effective income after rent loss, subtract operating costs, then subtract loan principal and interest. Review separate capital spending, reserves and taxes before deciding how much is available to spend.

questions.question: What is good cash flow for a rental property?
questions.answer: There is no universal monthly target. Evaluate cash invested, reserve needs, financing, vacancy risk and your required return. A small positive annual average can still leave months with cash shortfalls.

questions.question: Can a rental have positive NOI but negative cash flow?
questions.answer: Yes. In the higher-rate and higher-vacancy examples, operating income remains positive but full debt service exceeds NOI, creating negative cash flow.

questions.question: Does mortgage principal count as a cash expense?
questions.answer: It counts in debt service when estimating owner cash flow. It is not a property operating expense in the NOI calculation, and its tax treatment is a separate question.

questions.question: Does this cash-flow figure include a roof replacement reserve?
questions.answer: No dedicated capital reserve is subtracted by this tool. Add a separate reserve budget outside its first-year cash-flow figure or use the reserve-aware Cash-on-Cash Return Calculator.

questions.question: Is annual cash flow divided by twelve my actual monthly cash flow?
questions.answer: No. It is an average. Actual collection dates, vacancies and large bills can make individual months materially different.

questions.question: Can positive rental cash flow still produce an investment loss?
questions.answer: Yes. Acquisition costs, initial repairs, sale costs, declining value and taxes can outweigh operating cash receipts. The tool reports recurring cash flow separately from total investment profit.

limitations: One-year cases use zero growth and appreciation to isolate operating and financing changes; no market performance is asserted.
Before income tax, depreciation deductions, capital-gains tax and a separate capital replacement reserve.
Management applies to effective rent plus other income. Loan terms are fixed; rent and expense assumptions are not verified property records.

meta.title: How Are HELOC Payments Calculated? Draw and Repayment Examples
meta.heading: How Are HELOC Payments Calculated? Draw and Repayment Examples
meta.description: Calculate interest-only HELOC draw payments and amortizing repayment. Compare rates, terms, annual fees and closing costs using six reproducible scenarios.
meta.breadcrumb: How Are HELOC Payments Calculated? Draw and Repayment Examples
meta.cardIntro: Calculate interest-only HELOC draw payments and amortizing repayment. Compare rates, terms, annual fees and closing costs using six reproducible scenarios.

heloc.intro: HELOC payments depend on the outstanding balance, the applicable rate and the lender’s payment rules. An interest-only draw-period estimate differs from an amortizing repayment-period payment because the latter also pays down principal. Read your agreement for the actual minimum-payment formula, day count, fees, rate resets and any balloon requirement.
heloc.answer: Under our fixed-rate illustration, a $50,000 balance at 8% costs $333.33 monthly during a ten-year interest-only draw period, with no fees. Amortizing that unchanged balance over the following twenty years requires $418.22 monthly. The increase is about $84.89 after retaining precision, even though the interest rate has not changed.

sections.title: Calculate an interest-only draw payment from the amount borrowed
paragraphs: Use the outstanding borrowed balance rather than the entire approved credit limit. The simplified monthly interest is balance multiplied by the nominal annual rate divided by twelve. For $50,000 at 8%, this is 50,000 × 0.08 / 12, or $333.33 rounded to cents. Paying only that interest leaves the principal unchanged.

Our model assumes the full entered balance exists at the start and stays constant throughout draw. Actual HELOC users can borrow and repay at different dates, changing daily balances and interest charges. The calculator does not construct a schedule of new advances or replace your lender’s statement calculation.
sections.formula: Modeled monthly draw payment = outstanding balance × annual rate / 12 + allocated annual draw-period fee / 12

sections.title: Add principal amortization when repayment begins
paragraphs: At the end of the modeled draw period, new borrowing stops and the same balance is amortized. Let P be outstanding principal, i the annual rate divided by twelve and N the number of repayment months. Use the standard amortizing-payment formula, or P / N when the rate is zero.

The base twenty-year repayment term has 240 months and a $418.22 scheduled payment. Shortening repayment to ten years at the same 8% raises payment to $606.64, while reducing total interest. The ten-year draw period is separate from either repayment term; entering twenty repayment years does not include the draw years.
sections.formula: Repayment payment = P × i / [1 − (1 + i)^(−N)]; at 0% use P / N

sections.title: Separate repayment shock from a variable-rate reset
paragraphs: The base comparison shows a higher payment solely because principal amortization begins. A separate case holds the rate at 10% throughout: draw payment is $416.67 and twenty-year repayment is $482.51. That is a different constant-rate scenario, not a simulation of an actual 8%-to-10% reset on a chosen date.

CFPB guidance explains that HELOC rates are usually variable and some agreements can require a large payment at the end of draw. Our fully amortizing repayment assumption is only one structure. A real contract may use a different minimum-payment formula, rate cap, floor, conversion option or balloon. Stress-test rates as scenarios and confirm the actual contractual schedule.

sections.title: Keep annual fees, closing costs and borrowed principal distinct
paragraphs: With a $120 annual draw-period fee, this model allocates $10 to each draw month: the base average monthly outlay becomes $343.33. The annual fee stops in repayment under this model. Actual lender billing may collect the charge once a year, and actual fee rules can differ; a monthly allocation is a budgeting convention.

A separate case deducts a $1,000 closing cost from the $50,000 contractual balance. Cash disbursed is $49,000, while payments still amortize $50,000. Paying the same fee upfront instead would use outside cash. Neither treatment finances an extra fee on top of principal. Total interest remains unchanged by the fee treatment in these fixed-balance scenarios.

The tool also provides an estimated cash-flow annualized cost including its modeled fees. Do not treat that internal figure as your lender’s legally disclosed HELOC APR or a live quote. Compare disclosed rates, fee schedules and cash costs using the agreement and appropriate disclosure rules.

sections.title: Check both periods in a spreadsheet
paragraphs: For the no-fee base case, =50000*8%/12 gives monthly draw interest. Use =-PMT(8%/12,20*12,50000) for the positive monthly repayment amount. Keep the unrounded values when calculating differences; rounding each displayed payment first can change a difference by a cent.

At zero interest, the draw interest is zero and twenty-year repayment is $50,000 / 240, or $208.33 monthly. Zero interest does not eliminate principal repayment. Across the base thirty-year combined schedule, the model calculates $90,372.81 total interest before fees. That total assumes the full balance remains outstanding throughout draw and excludes further advances.

sections.title: Use the estimate to ask better questions before borrowing
paragraphs: Ask how the lender calculates minimum payments, when rates reset, whether fees persist after draw, whether principal is required during draw and whether a balloon can become due. Compare a HELOC with a home equity loan using the same borrowed amount and relevant repayment horizon rather than comparing an interest-only payment with a principal-and-interest payment.

A calculated payment is not borrowing approval or evidence of affordability. Your home secures the obligation. CFPB warns that failing to repay can put it at risk, and access to further draws may be restricted under specified conditions. The model does not assess your income, credit, collateral value or ability to meet a higher future payment.

heloc.chartAlt: Interest-only draw and amortizing repayment payments for the same $50,000 balance under three rate and repayment-term scenarios.
heloc.chartCaption: Each scenario uses a constant rate, the full balance at the start, no new advances and no fees in the chart. The table separately tests fees, deducted closing costs and zero interest.

questions.question: How are interest-only HELOC payments calculated?
questions.answer: A simplified equal-month estimate is outstanding balance × nominal annual rate / 12. Actual statements can use daily balances, lender-specific day counts and additional minimum-payment requirements.

questions.question: Why does the payment rise after the draw period?
questions.answer: Repayment can require principal as well as interest. In the base example, the rate stays at 8% while monthly payment rises from $333.33 interest only to $418.22 amortizing over twenty years.

questions.question: Are payments based on the credit limit or the borrowed balance?
questions.answer: This calculation uses the outstanding borrowed balance. It does not charge interest on an unused credit limit, although actual accounts may have separate fees or minimum-draw conditions.

questions.question: Does the calculator simulate future variable rates?
questions.answer: No. Each scenario holds one entered rate constant throughout draw and repayment. Repeating the calculation at a higher rate is sensitivity testing, not a forecast or dated reset simulation.

questions.question: Does paying a deducted closing cost reduce the contractual principal?
questions.answer: No. In the $1,000 deducted-fee example, you receive $49,000 but still owe the entered $50,000 balance. Financing a fee on top would be a different transaction.

questions.question: What happens if the HELOC has no interest?
questions.answer: With a 0% rate and no fees, modeled draw interest is zero, but the $50,000 principal still requires $208.33 monthly over a twenty-year repayment period.

questions.question: Does every HELOC have a fully amortizing repayment period?
questions.answer: No. Actual agreements can have different minimum-payment rules, terms or balloon requirements. Review the lender’s disclosures; this model assumes fully amortizing repayment.

limitations: Constant borrowed balance during draw, one fixed rate per scenario, equal monthly periods and fully amortizing repayment; no daily-balance history or new advances.
Annual fees apply only during draw and are allocated monthly; closing fees reduce net proceeds without increasing contractual principal.
Payments, cash-flow annualized cost and fee assumptions are estimates, not lender disclosures, approval or affordability assessments.

meta.title: How to Calculate Stock Profit: Fees, Dividends and Break-Even
meta.heading: How to Calculate Stock Profit: Fees, Dividends and Break-Even
meta.description: Calculate stock profit and percentage return after trading fees and cash dividends. Includes six checked examples, fractional shares and the break-even sale-price formula.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Stock Profit: Fees, Dividends and Break-Even
meta.cardIntro: Calculate stock profit and percentage return after trading fees and cash dividends. Includes six checked examples, fractional shares and the break-even sale-price formula.

stockprofit.intro: To calculate profit on a long stock position sold in full, subtract total purchase cost from net sale proceeds plus any unreinvested cash dividends. Include fees on both transactions. Then divide profit by the purchase cost to calculate the return on that cost. This is an economic cash reconciliation before income tax, not a prediction of a future stock price.
stockprofit.answer: Buying 100 shares at $50 with a $5 purchase fee costs $5,005. Selling all 100 at $60 with a $5 sale fee receives $5,995. With no dividends, net profit is $990 and return on purchase cost is 19.7802%. Recovering the original cost requires a $50.10 sale price per share under those same fixed fees.

sections.title: Separate gross trade values from cash actually paid and received
paragraphs: Multiply shares by the purchase price to obtain gross purchase value, then add the buy fee once. Multiply shares by the sale price to obtain gross sale value, then subtract the sale fee once. In the base case, the $1,000 gross price-change gain becomes $990 after $10 total fees.

Fees expressed in USD are total amounts for each transaction in this model, not charges per share. Percentage fees instead apply to that side’s gross trade value. For example, a 0.5% buy fee on $5,000 is $25; a 1% sell fee on $6,000 is $60. Use the fee rule shown on your trade confirmation rather than entering a percentage as a dollar amount.
sections.formula: Profit = shares × sale price − sell fee + unreinvested cash dividends − (shares × buy price + buy fee)

sections.title: Use purchase cost as the percentage-return denominator
paragraphs: Divide the $990 net profit by $5,005 purchase cost, then multiply by 100. The result differs from the 20% price change because the percentage incorporates the specified trading fees. Profit in dollars and percentage return answer different questions; a bigger dollar gain can require much more capital.

The tool has no holding dates, so this percentage is not annualized. The same endpoint profit over one year and five years would have different annualized returns. For compatible endpoint comparisons, use the linked annualized-return guide; for multiple external cash flows, review a cash-flow return method rather than treating all money as invested at the start.
sections.formula: Return on purchase cost (%) = net profit / positive total purchase cost × 100

sections.title: Include cash dividends once and keep reinvestment separate
paragraphs: The percentage-fee case adds $200 cumulative unreinvested cash dividends. Its $5,025 purchase cost and $6,140 total receipts give $1,115 profit. Another case holds sale price at the $50 purchase price but adds $200 dividends; after the two $5 fees, profit is $190 despite no price appreciation.

Enter actual cumulative cash dividends for the position, not an annual yield percentage. Do not add dividends again if your prices or share quantities already reflect a dividend-reinvestment or total-return series. Reinvested dividends change the purchase history and share count; the DRIP Calculator is designed for a disclosed reinvestment projection.

sections.title: Solve for the sale price needed to recover the modeled cost
paragraphs: With a fixed sale fee, add that fee to purchase cost, subtract unreinvested cash dividends, and divide by shares. For the base case, ($5,005 + $5) / 100 gives $50.10. With $200 dividends already received, the same fixed-fee break-even threshold becomes $48.10.

With a percentage sale fee, divide by shares multiplied by one minus the fee fraction instead. The purchase fee is already part of total purchase cost and must not be added again. Special conditions need explicit handling: a 100% sale fee removes all gross sale receipts, and sufficient prior dividends can recover cost even at zero sale price.
sections.formula: Break-even sale price = (purchase cost + fixed sell fee − cash dividends) / [shares × (1 − percentage sell fee)]

sections.title: Retain losses and check fractional-share assumptions
paragraphs: Selling the base 100-share position at $40 produces a $1,010 loss after fees. Fractional shares work through the same multiplication: 2.5 shares bought at $40 and sold at $45 with $1 fees on each side produce $10.50 profit on $101 cost.

The zero-sale-price case still charges the entered fixed $5 sale fee. That makes the modeled loss $5,010, slightly larger than purchase cost, because additional cash pays the sale fee. This is a boundary check of the entered fee rule, not a claim that all worthless holdings are liquidated that way. Actual broker treatment may differ.

sections.title: Reproduce the reconciliation in a spreadsheet
paragraphs: For the base case, =100*60-5-(100*50+5) returns $990. Divide that cell by =100*50+5 and format the result as a percentage. Keep the share count, each fee rule and dividend amount in separate cells so a price sensitivity does not accidentally change unrelated inputs.

The calculator assumes one unleveraged long position sold in full, one currency and manually entered prices. It does not handle short selling, options, margin interest, partial-sale tax lots, splits or wash-sale adjustments. Taxable gain can differ from this economic result; use broker records and applicable reporting rules for a tax return.

stockprofit.chartAlt: Profit or loss at hypothetical sale prices of forty, fifty and sixty dollars for one hundred shares bought at fifty dollars, with five-dollar fees on each side.
stockprofit.chartCaption: The chart holds quantity, purchase price and fixed fees constant; only sale price changes. No dividends are included in the chart.

questions.question: How do I calculate stock profit percentage?
questions.answer: Subtract full purchase cost from net sale receipts plus eligible cash dividends, then divide by positive purchase cost. Format that ratio as a percentage; it is not annualized by this tool.

questions.question: Are trading fees per share or per transaction?
questions.answer: USD fees are total transaction fees here. Percentage fees apply to each trade’s gross value. Convert a broker’s per-share charge to a total amount before entering it.

questions.question: Can an unchanged stock price still produce a profit?
questions.answer: Yes, if unreinvested cash dividends exceed the included transaction costs. The checked unchanged-price example earns $190 before income tax.

questions.question: Can I calculate profit on fractional shares?
questions.answer: Yes. The model accepts fractional positive quantities and uses the same cash reconciliation. Confirm actual broker execution and fee rules separately.

questions.question: Does this show my taxable capital gain?
questions.answer: No. Tax basis adjustments, holding-period treatment, wash sales and partial-sale identification are outside this economic before-tax calculation.

questions.question: Can I use the calculator to forecast a stock price?
questions.answer: No. Sale prices are manually entered scenarios, not market quotes, forecasts or recommendations.

limitations: One long, unleveraged position sold in full in USD; no partial sales, tax-lot methods, corporate actions or live prices.
Cash dividends are unreinvested and entered once. Fees follow the specific fixed or percentage rules supplied.
Return requires positive purchase cost and is not annualized. Income taxes and borrowing are excluded.

meta.title: How to Calculate Average Stock Price: Weighted Cost and Adding Shares
meta.heading: How to Calculate Average Stock Price: Weighted Cost and Adding Shares
meta.description: Calculate quantity-weighted stock cost with fees. Compare averaging down, averaging up and fractional purchases without confusing lower unit cost with recovered losses.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Average Stock Price: Weighted Cost and Adding Shares
meta.cardIntro: Calculate quantity-weighted stock cost with fees. Compare averaging down, averaging up and fractional purchases without confusing lower unit cost with recovered losses.

stockaverage.intro: Average stock acquisition cost is total purchase spending, including entered purchase fees, divided by total shares. Weight each price by the quantity bought. This economic average describes an intact position built from purchases; it is not automatically the tax basis method for a later partial sale.
stockaverage.answer: Buying 100 shares at $50 and 50 shares at $40 with $5 fees on each purchase costs $7,010 for 150 shares. Average cost including fees is $46.7333 per share. The simple midpoint of $45 is wrong because the two purchases contain different numbers of shares.

sections.title: Weight purchase prices by the shares acquired
paragraphs: Calculate each lot’s gross purchase value by multiplying quantity by price. Sum those values and the fixed buy fees, then divide by total shares. For the unequal-purchase example, gross spending is $5,000 + $2,000, fees are $10 and total shares are 150.

Without fees, the quantity-weighted purchase price is $7,000 / 150, or $46.6667. Including fees raises it to $7,010 / 150, or $46.7333. The calculator reports both measures so you can distinguish price weighting from transaction costs. A simple average of prices works only under compatible equal quantities and does not automatically include fees.
sections.formula: Average cost per share = [Σ(quantity × purchase price) + Σ(total buy fees)] / Σ(quantity)

sections.title: A lower average price does not erase the existing dollar loss
paragraphs: Start with 100 shares bought at $50 plus a $5 fee. At a comparison price of $40, the position is worth $4,000 versus $5,005 purchase cost: a $1,005 unrealized loss. Buying another 100 shares at $40 plus a $5 fee brings total cost to $9,010 and quantity to 200.

Average cost falls from $50.05 to $45.05, but the position’s $8,000 comparison value is still $1,010 below cost. The original loss has not vanished; the new fee adds another $5 loss at the unchanged comparison price. A smaller percentage loss can coexist with the same or larger dollar loss and more capital committed.

sections.title: Compare cash committed as well as cost per share
paragraphs: The chart shows both the unit cost and total invested cash for the original and added-share cases. Lower cost per share is only one consequence of adding a cheaper purchase. The additional $4,005 is new capital exposed to the same security, not a refund of the previous purchase.

This arithmetic does not determine whether adding shares is appropriate. A stock can keep falling, concentration can increase and future recovery is uncertain. Do not infer diversification or improved business prospects from a lower average. The tool performs the calculation without recommending a purchase.

sections.title: Averaging up and fractional shares use the same formula
paragraphs: Adding 100 shares at $60 instead of $40 produces $11,010 total cost and a $55.05 average, including two $5 fees. At the same $40 comparison price, the modeled unrealized loss is $3,010. The formula works regardless of whether a later price is higher or lower; the decision to buy is separate.

Fractional quantities also carry their actual weight. Buying 1.5 shares at $40 and 0.5 shares at $60 with $1 fees on each purchase costs $92 for two shares. Average cost is $46. A $45 comparison price gives a $2 unrealized loss before selling fees and tax.

sections.title: An optional comparison price is a scenario, not a live quote
paragraphs: Position value equals total shares multiplied by the manually entered comparison price. Unrealized gain or loss is that value less total purchase cost. A blank comparison-price field lets you calculate average cost without inventing a market valuation; entering zero intentionally represents zero comparison value.

The comparison excludes selling fees, dividends, interest and taxes. Use the Stock Profit Calculator for a full sale scenario with its disclosed fee and dividend assumptions. Do not combine different securities or currencies into one average, and do not mix split-adjusted prices with unadjusted share quantities.

sections.title: Check the result without treating it as a tax-lot ledger
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, use =(100*50+50*40+5+5)/(100+50) for the unequal-purchase example. For a column of purchases, SUMPRODUCT(share_range,price_range) plus SUM(fee_range), divided by SUM(share_range), gives the same weighted method. Keep full precision internally and format the final cost per share.

The calculator records purchases only. It does not deplete sold lots, implement FIFO or specific identification, adjust for wash sales, or track reinvested dividends and corporate actions. IRS average-basis eligibility depends on the security and acquisition arrangement; this general economic average is not a tax-method election. Keep broker records and use the appropriate reporting guidance.

stockaverage.chartAlt: Two panels compare cost per share and total invested cash before and after adding one hundred shares at forty dollars.
stockaverage.chartCaption: The added-share case lowers unit cost but increases committed cash. At the same $40 comparison price, dollar loss changes from $1,005 to $1,010 because of the new $5 fee.

questions.question: How do I calculate average stock price for unequal purchases?
questions.answer: Multiply each purchase price by its share quantity, add the resulting spending and purchase fees, then divide by total shares. Do not give different-sized purchases equal weight.

questions.question: Does averaging down reduce my existing dollar loss?
questions.answer: Not by itself. Buying at the current comparison price adds value and cost together; the existing dollar loss remains, with any additional fee increasing it.

questions.question: Can I average up instead of down?
questions.answer: Yes. The weighted calculation also handles later purchases at higher prices. It describes entered costs and does not recommend either strategy.

questions.question: Does the average include commissions?
questions.answer: The headline cost includes the fixed total USD fee entered for each purchase. A separate weighted purchase-price metric excludes those fees.

questions.question: Can I leave the comparison price blank?
questions.answer: Yes. Average cost can be calculated without a market-value estimate. A blank price and an explicit zero price represent different inputs.

questions.question: Can I use this average for a partial stock-sale tax return?
questions.answer: Not automatically. This is a purchases-only economic average, with no tax-lot depletion or basis adjustments. Applicable tax methods and broker records require separate review.

limitations: One security and one currency, purchases only; no sales, tax-lot depletion, splits or reinvested distributions.
Fees are total USD amounts per purchase. Optional valuation uses an entered comparison price, not a live quote.
Lower cost per share is not a risk reduction or recovery guarantee; additional purchases commit additional capital.

sources.label: IRS Publication 550: basis and eligible average-basis arrangements
Investor.gov: transaction and ongoing investment costs

meta.title: How to Calculate IRR: Cash-Flow Timing, Excel and Multiple Roots
meta.heading: How to Calculate IRR: Cash-Flow Timing, Excel and Multiple Roots
meta.description: Calculate IRR from signed cash flows and correct timing. Includes six checked examples, Excel formulas, zero periods, negative returns and a two-IRR case.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate IRR: Cash-Flow Timing, Excel and Multiple Roots
meta.cardIntro: Calculate IRR from signed cash flows and correct timing. Includes six checked examples, Excel formulas, zero periods, negative returns and a two-IRR case.

irr.intro: Internal rate of return is a discount rate at which a specified cash-flow stream has zero net present value. The cash amounts, signs and payment dates all matter. For equally spaced annual flows, IRR is an annual rate. A percentage that solves the equation is not a measure of investment safety or a complete comparison of projects.
irr.answer: An initial $1,000 outflow followed by a $1,210 receipt one year later has 21% annual IRR. Receiving the same $1,210 after two years, with no year-one receipt, has 10% annual IRR. The total dollar gain is unchanged, but its timing changes the annualized cash-flow return.

sections.title: Set net present value to zero
paragraphs: Write the initial investment as a time-zero outflow, then include each subsequent net receipt or payment at the correct time. The annual equation discounts year-one cash by 1 + r, year-two cash by (1 + r)^2 and so on. A candidate r is an IRR only if the resulting sum is zero.

For a single receipt, the equation can be solved directly: (ending receipt / initial outflow)^(1 / years) − 1. With several intervening flows, a numerical method is usually needed. The checked unequal-receipt case invests $10,000 initially and receives $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 at successive year ends, producing about 8.8963% annual IRR.
sections.formula: NPV(r) = CF0 + CF1/(1+r) + CF2/(1+r)^2 + … + CFN/(1+r)^N; an IRR satisfies NPV(r) = 0

sections.title: Enter initial investment once and retain zero periods
paragraphs: In this tool, the Initial investment field takes a positive dollar amount and converts it to the negative time-zero outflow. In Unequal Annual Cash Flows mode, enter only later amounts starting at year one. For the two-year $1,210 example, enter initial 1000 and subsequent flows 0, 1210.

Omitting the zero moves the receipt to year one and changes the answer to 21%. Repeating the initial investment in the later-flow field also changes the actual investment being modeled. Commas separate cash-flow entries here; write 10000 rather than 10,000 for a single amount.

sections.title: Unequal amounts are not the same as irregular dates
paragraphs: The Unequal Annual Cash Flows mode accepts varying amounts, but they are still one year apart. It is not date-based XIRR. For actual uneven calendar dates, use the dated mode in Average Return Calculator and follow its documented date convention.

The separate Fixed Cash Flow mode supports disclosed payment frequencies and beginning/end timing, and its headline rates are effective annual IRRs. A monthly spreadsheet IRR, by contrast, is per month unless you annualize it. Compare equivalent timing and units before deciding a spreadsheet disagrees with the website.

sections.title: A cash-flow stream can have more than one IRR
paragraphs: The hypothetical series −100, +230, −132 at times 0, 1 and 2 has two positive annual roots: 10% and 20%. Substituting either into the NPV equation gives zero. A later large outflow creates a nonconventional sign pattern, so a solver returning one rate does not establish a unique answer.

The site reports detected roots and warns when there is more than one. Its numerical search is bounded and does not guarantee every mathematically possible root was found. Repeated and nearly repeated roots are especially sensitive. Review the complete pattern and NPV at a justified required return rather than choosing whichever root looks more attractive.

sections.title: Check IRR and NPV in Excel or Google Sheets
paragraphs: For annual cash flows −1000, 0, 1210 in cells A1:A3, =IRR(A1:A3) returns 10%. Check the root using =A1+NPV(10%,A2:A3); the initial flow is added separately because the ordinary spreadsheet NPV function treats its listed flows as future periods.

For −100, 230, −132, try different IRR guesses and inspect both roots rather than assuming one default guess proves uniqueness. Spreadsheet iteration and site numerical search can find different members of a multiple-root set. For monthly flows, annualize a periodic rate p using (1+p)^12 − 1, not p multiplied by twelve.

sections.title: A high IRR is not the same as more profit or less risk
paragraphs: The $900 receipt after a $1,000 one-year investment gives −10% IRR; the tool retains the negative result. A larger project can generate more dollar profit with a lower rate, and projects can differ in risk, duration, financing and required capital. IRR alone does not settle those choices.

MIRR makes separate financing and reinvestment assumptions explicit and can provide a different analytical view. It is still assumption-dependent, not a guaranteed achieved return. Use cash budgets, NPV with a considered discount rate and the actual project context alongside any single rate.

irr.chartAlt: Annual IRR for one-thousand-dollar initial investments with a 1210-dollar receipt after one or two years, or a 900-dollar receipt after one year.
irr.chartCaption: The first two charted cases differ only in receipt timing. The table also includes unequal annual receipts and a series with two detected positive roots.

questions.question: How do I calculate IRR in Excel?
questions.answer: Put all signed, equally spaced flows in order, including time zero and explicit zero periods, then use IRR(range). The result is per cash-flow period; match that period before comparing annual rates.

questions.question: Why can the same cash flows have two IRRs?
questions.answer: Nonconventional cash-flow patterns can make the NPV equation cross zero more than once. The checked −100, 230, −132 series has roots at 10% and 20%.

questions.question: Is the Unequal Annual Cash Flows mode XIRR?
questions.answer: No. Amounts may differ, but the model places them at successive year ends. Actual irregular dates need a date-based model.

questions.question: Why must I keep a zero-flow year?
questions.answer: Zero preserves the cash-flow date. Removing it moves all later amounts earlier and can materially increase the calculated annual rate.

questions.question: Can IRR be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. Receiving $900 after investing $1,000 one year earlier gives −10% IRR in the checked example.

questions.question: Does the highest IRR identify the best investment?
questions.answer: No. IRR does not establish dollar profitability, risk, scale or suitability, and multiple roots can make a single-rate comparison ambiguous.

limitations: Annual unequal-amount cases have fixed year-end dates; no tax, fees or inflation are inferred from unspecified amounts.
Numerical root detection is bounded and can miss roots; the presence of a reported rate does not prove uniqueness or investment quality.
Cases use independent Decimal calculations, including explicit checks of both known polynomial roots; no market backtest is claimed.
