meta.title: How to Calculate MIRR: Financing, Reinvestment and Periods
meta.heading: How to Calculate MIRR: Financing, Reinvestment and Periods
meta.description: Calculate modified internal rate of return from outflow present value and inflow terminal value. Includes seven checked cases, quarterly conversion and Excel formulas.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate MIRR: Financing, Reinvestment and Periods
meta.cardIntro: Calculate modified internal rate of return from outflow present value and inflow terminal value. Includes seven checked cases, quarterly conversion and Excel formulas.

mirr.intro: Modified internal rate of return separates the assumed cost of financing negative cash flows from the assumed reinvestment of positive cash flows. Discount payments to time zero, compound receipts to the final period and solve the rate connecting those two totals. Both assumptions must match the spacing of the entered flows.
mirr.answer: For annual flows −$10,000, $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 at years 0–3, an 8% financing assumption and 10% reinvestment assumption give $10,000 present-value outflows and $13,030 terminal-value receipts. MIRR is approximately 9.2232% annually. These are chosen rate assumptions, not returns the calculator can guarantee.

sections.title: Count cash-flow intervals, not entries
paragraphs: Enter the first signed amount at time zero and one amount at each equally spaced date thereafter. Four entries at years 0, 1, 2 and 3 contain three compounding intervals, not four. Keep explicit zero amounts for dates with no cash movement.

This tool requires one number per line, with no thousands separators or labels. It rejects an internal blank line rather than silently shifting later cash flows. At least one positive and one negative amount are required. Actual uneven dates cannot be represented merely by labeling a list quarterly or annually.

sections.title: Calculate outflow present value and receipt terminal value
paragraphs: Discount each negative cash flow at the financing rate from its own date back to time zero. Add the magnitudes to obtain the outflow present value. Compound each positive cash flow at the reinvestment rate from its own date forward to the final period.

In the base series, the only negative payment is at time zero, so its present value is $10,000 regardless of the financing rate. Terminal receipts are $3,000 × 1.10^2 + $4,000 × 1.10 + $5,000 = $13,030. The last receipt is already at the horizon and receives no extra reinvestment period.
sections.formula: MIRR per period = (terminal value of positive flows / absolute present value of negative flows)^(1 / number of intervals) − 1

sections.title: Test the effect of a different reinvestment assumption
paragraphs: With the same annual project cash flows, reducing reinvestment from 10% to 5% lowers terminal receipts to $12,507.50 and MIRR to about 7.7433%. At 0% reinvestment, receipts sum to $12,000 and MIRR is about 6.2659%. The chart isolates this single assumption.

The project’s entered receipts did not change. The different rates come from different treatment of cash available before the horizon. The assumed reinvestment return may not be achievable, and the modeled terminal pool is not an actual account balance observed in the market. A more favorable assumption is not evidence that a project improved.

sections.title: Later negative cash flows make the financing assumption matter
paragraphs: A separate series invests $10,000 initially and another $2,000 at year one, then receives $6,000 at year two and $9,000 at year three. At 8% financing, present-value outflows are approximately $11,851.85; at 20%, they are $11,666.67. Both cases retain the same 10% reinvestment assumption and $15,600 terminal receipts.

Their MIRRs are about 9.5922% and 10.1690%, respectively. The higher financing assumption discounts the later outlay more strongly, lowering its present-value magnitude in this formula. Do not interpret the higher computed MIRR as evidence that more expensive borrowing is beneficial. No actual loan balance or payment schedule has been modeled.

sections.title: Convert annual assumptions for quarterly or monthly cash flows
paragraphs: Both site rate fields are effective annual rates. For quarterly spacing, convert an annual decimal rate R to (1+R)^(1/4) − 1; for monthly spacing use the twelfth root. Dividing an effective annual rate by four or twelve is not the equivalent compound rate.

The two-quarter example has −$1,000 at time zero, $100 after one quarter and $1,100 after two quarters. With 8% annual financing and 10% annual reinvestment, periodic MIRR is about 9.6545%, while effective annual MIRR is about 44.5793%. The latter annualizes a six-month scenario; it is not a full year of observed earnings.
sections.formula: Effective annual MIRR = (1 + MIRR per period)^(periods per year) − 1

sections.title: Match Excel MIRR and preserve the interpretation
paragraphs: For the annual base series in A1:A4, use =MIRR(A1:A4,8%,10%). For quarterly flows, use =MIRR(range,(1+8%)^(1/4)-1,(1+10%)^(1/4)-1), then annualize that periodic result with the fourth power. The cash-flow order, zeros and number of intervals must also match.

Under this defined financing/reinvestment construction, a valid positive present-value magnitude and terminal-value pool produce one periodic MIRR greater than −100%. That does not make it the same as IRR or an NPV decision rule. A checked −1000, 900 annual series has −10% MIRR; losses are not floored at zero. Review assumptions, project scale and risk before using the rate in a decision.

mirr.chartAlt: Effective annual MIRR for the same three-year cash-flow stream at zero, five and ten percent annual reinvestment assumptions.
mirr.chartCaption: Only reinvestment changes in the chart. The table separately tests a later outlay, negative return and quarterly spacing.

questions.question: What is the difference between MIRR and IRR?
questions.answer: IRR solves the cash-flow NPV equation and can have multiple roots. This MIRR construction separately specifies financing and reinvestment rates, then links outflow present value to inflow terminal value.

questions.question: How do I calculate MIRR in Excel?
questions.answer: Use MIRR(values,finance_rate,reinvest_rate) with rates per cash-flow period. For nonannual site inputs, convert the entered effective annual assumptions to equivalent period rates first.

questions.question: Why does a financing-rate change sometimes have no effect?
questions.answer: If every negative cash flow is at time zero, there is no later negative payment to discount. The base guide case has exactly that structure.

questions.question: Does a higher assumed reinvestment rate prove a better project?
questions.answer: No. It changes the modeled terminal value of interim receipts while the project cash flows stay fixed. Real reinvestment returns can differ.

questions.question: Can MIRR be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. The checked $1,000 outlay followed by a $900 receipt one year later gives −10% with zero financing and reinvestment assumptions.

questions.question: Are the displayed monthly or quarterly results annualized?
questions.answer: The tool reports both a per-period MIRR and a compounded effective annual MIRR. Use the correct output and horizon for your comparison.

limitations: Equal annual, quarterly or monthly spacing, with annual effective rate inputs; no actual irregular dates or inferred loan schedules.
Financing and reinvestment rates are explicit assumptions. Taxes, fees and inflation are not automatically added.
One computed MIRR under this construction does not replace NPV, risk analysis or a check of real-world financing and reinvestment availability.

meta.title: How to Calculate Seller Financing: Payments, Balloon and Maturity
meta.heading: How to Calculate Seller Financing: Payments, Balloon and Maturity
meta.description: Calculate owner financing installments and the final balloon. Compare amortization, maturity, interest-only and zero-interest notes with six reproducible examples.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Seller Financing: Payments, Balloon and Maturity
meta.cardIntro: Calculate owner financing installments and the final balloon. Compare amortization, maturity, interest-only and zero-interest notes with six reproducible examples.

seller.intro: Seller financing, also called owner financing in this calculator, means the purchase financing is supplied through the seller’s note rather than modeled as a standard third-party mortgage. To calculate the payment schedule, separate the financed principal, interest rate, amortization length and contractual maturity. A manageable regular installment can still leave a large final obligation.
seller.answer: A $300,000 purchase with $60,000 down leaves a $240,000 note. At 6% nominal annual interest and thirty-year amortization, the regular monthly installment is $1,438.92. If the note matures after installment 60, residual principal is $223,330.46 and total due that final month is $224,769.38. The down payment is separate from the debt schedule.

sections.title: Amortization length and maturity answer different questions
paragraphs: Amortization length sets the size of the regular installment. A thirty-year amortization schedule would extinguish the debt over 360 monthly payments if allowed to run to completion under these assumptions. Contractual maturity tells you when the note must actually be settled.

In the base example, maturity is month 60 even though installments are sized over 360 months. The first sixty installments therefore do not repay the whole principal. Do not enter a five-year maturity as a five-year amortization unless that is truly how the contract sizes the monthly payment.

sections.title: Calculate the installment from the financed amount
paragraphs: Subtract down payment from price before applying the payment formula: $300,000 − $60,000 = $240,000. Convert the 6% nominal annual rate to 0.005 per month and use 360 amortization months. At zero interest, the amortizing installment is principal divided by the amortization-month count.

The model uses end-of-month payments, equal monthly periods and fixed interest. No points, closing costs, property tax, insurance, penalties or extra principal payments are included. The entered purchase-price cash total includes only down payment and loan payments, so it is not the full cost of acquiring and owning the home.
sections.formula: Monthly installment = P × i / [1 − (1 + i)^(−N)]; at i = 0 use P / N

sections.title: Pay the final scheduled installment before measuring residual principal
paragraphs: At maturity, the schedule first accrues interest and makes that month’s ordinary installment. It then settles the principal still outstanding. The output called Balloon principal after final installment is only that residual principal; Total due in final month adds the final scheduled installment to it.

For the base note, adding the two displayed components gives $224,769.38 due in month 60. Paying only the residual misses the installment; adding a full principal balance before and after the installment counts part of the debt twice. Internal precision is retained, so separately rounded components can sometimes sum a cent differently from an internally calculated total.
sections.formula: Final-month amount due = scheduled installment for that month + principal remaining after that installment

sections.title: Compare the same note under different repayment structures
paragraphs: Extending maturity to month 120 keeps the $1,438.92 regular payment when amortization remains thirty years. Residual principal falls to $200,845.74, but the note has accumulated $133,516.29 interest through maturity rather than $69,665.73 through month 60. More time is not a free reduction in cost.

A fifteen-year amortization at the original month-60 maturity raises the installment to $2,025.26 and reduces residual principal to $182,421.84. Interest-only at 6% needs $1,200 monthly but leaves all $240,000 principal due after the final interest installment. Its final-month total is $241,200. The chart compares both regular payments and residual balances.

sections.title: Zero interest and full amortization still require principal settlement
paragraphs: At 0% with thirty-year amortization and month-60 maturity, regular principal installments are $666.67 before display rounding. Residual principal is $200,000, and the final month requires $200,666.67. Zero interest does not waive the unpaid purchase debt.

If the fixed-rate note instead runs through all 360 amortization months, no material balloon remains after the final installment. This is a different maturity setting, not the result of assuming that a short balloon note will automatically renew.

sections.title: Reproduce the schedule and review what the calculation cannot decide
paragraphs: For the base installment, use =-PMT(6%/12,30*12,240000). In a monthly ledger, interest is opening principal × 6%/12; principal reduction is installment minus interest. Carry the closing balance forward. After row 60, add remaining principal to that row’s scheduled payment.

CFPB warns that refinancing a balloon can become unavailable if finances or property values deteriorate. This tool does not determine legal eligibility, licensing, lien priority, title ownership, wraparound structures or installment-sale taxes. A schedule is not proof that a proposed contract is lawful, affordable or refinanceable.

seller.chartAlt: Two panels compare monthly installments and month-sixty residual principal for thirty-year amortization, fifteen-year amortization and an interest-only note.
seller.chartCaption: All charted cases finance $240,000 at 6% and settle after installment 60. Final-month total includes both that installment and residual principal.

questions.question: Are seller financing and owner financing the same here?
questions.answer: Yes. Both names refer to the fixed-rate seller-provided real-estate note modeled by this tool. Actual documentation and legal treatment require separate review.

questions.question: Is the balloon equal to the original financed amount?
questions.answer: Only in the interest-only example. An amortizing note pays down some principal before maturity, so its residual balloon is smaller.

questions.question: Does the final-month total include the regular payment?
questions.answer: Yes. It includes that month’s scheduled installment plus the residual principal calculated after the installment. Do not add the installment a second time.

questions.question: Can I use a thirty-year amortization with a five-year maturity?
questions.answer: The model can calculate that schedule: the regular installment uses 360 months, while residual principal becomes due after month 60. It does not establish whether a contract with those terms is legally permitted.

questions.question: What happens at zero interest?
questions.answer: Principal still must be repaid. In an amortizing note, divide principal by amortization months; in an interest-only note the regular interest payment is zero but principal remains due at maturity.

questions.question: Can I assume I will refinance the balloon?
questions.answer: No. Future credit, property value, rates and lender availability can change. A possible refinancing is not a funded payment plan or a guarantee.

limitations: One fixed-rate USD note, end-of-month payments; no taxes, fees, insurance, extra payments, daily accrual or changing rates.
Maturity and amortization are separate inputs. Final settlement pays residual principal exactly once.
No legal eligibility, title, tax or future-refinancing determination is provided.

meta.title: How to Calculate House-Flipping Profit: Costs, Cash and Break-Even
meta.heading: How to Calculate House-Flipping Profit: Costs, Cash and Break-Even
meta.description: Estimate fix-and-flip profit after renovation, holding, financing and selling costs. Compare five checked projects, sale delays, losses and cash requirements.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate House-Flipping Profit: Costs, Cash and Break-Even
meta.cardIntro: Estimate fix-and-flip profit after renovation, holding, financing and selling costs. Compare five checked projects, sale delays, losses and cash requirements.

flip.intro: Calculate house-flipping profit by subtracting the full purchase, renovation, carrying, financing and selling budget from the assumed sale price. Then calculate cash funding separately: an acquisition loan supplies financing but must be repaid at sale. A project can show an attractive sale-price spread while having little profit after the omitted costs are restored.
flip.answer: The base hypothetical project buys for $150,000 and sells for $250,000. After purchase closing, renovation including contingency, six months of carrying costs, acquisition interest and points, and selling costs, profit is $28,500 before income tax. Pre-sale cash funding is $85,000 under the stated $120,000 acquisition-only loan, not the $100,000 purchase-to-sale price spread.

sections.title: Build a complete cost reconciliation before calculating ROI
paragraphs: The base project pays $4,500 acquisition closing costs and budgets $35,000 renovation plus 10% contingency, giving $38,500 renovation funding. Six months of $600 non-debt holding costs adds $3,600. Those holding costs represent the entered taxes, insurance, utilities and other carrying budget.

The $120,000 interest-only acquisition loan costs $6,000 interest at 10% annually for six months, plus $2,400 in upfront points. Adding purchase price and all these amounts gives $205,000 project cost before selling costs. Interest is entered separately from holding costs so it is not counted twice.

sections.title: Subtract selling costs and repay loan principal only once
paragraphs: At a $250,000 assumed sale price, 6% percentage selling costs plus $1,500 fixed selling costs total $16,500. Profit is $250,000 − $16,500 − $205,000 = $28,500. Net sale cash after repaying $120,000 principal is $113,500; subtracting the $85,000 pre-sale cash funding reconciles to the same profit.

Loan principal is not an extra expense on top of the purchase price. Borrowing reduces initial cash funding, and repayment reduces sale cash. Adding principal repayment again to project expenses understates profit. Interest and points, in contrast, are financing costs that really do reduce the modeled profit.
sections.formula: Project profit = sale price − selling costs − purchase − closing − renovation − holding costs − interest − points

sections.title: Cash required before sale is different from profit and closing-day cash
paragraphs: The model’s cumulative pre-sale cash funding is project cost before selling costs minus the acquisition loan: $205,000 − $120,000 = $85,000. All renovation cash is budgeted upfront; holding costs and interest accrue in monthly cash funding. This is not a staged construction-draw or contractor-payment model.

Project cash-on-cash ROI is $28,500 / $85,000, about 33.5294%. It is an unannualized single-project ratio. It is not a cap rate, IRR or guaranteed six-month investment return. A different financing structure can change cash committed and profit; compare both outputs, not just the ratio.

sections.title: Test delays, renovation overruns and a lower sale price
paragraphs: Delaying the sale from month six to month nine adds $1,800 non-debt carrying costs and $3,000 acquisition interest. Profit falls by $4,800 to $23,700, while cash funding rises to $89,800. The entered sale price stays at $250,000; no higher future sale price is assumed to rescue the delay.

Raising the renovation budget to $50,000 before the same 10% contingency makes renovation funding $55,000 and profit $12,000. A separate sale-price-only case uses $210,000 and produces a $9,100 loss. These are controlled stress scenarios, not forecasts of repair costs or local market values.

sections.title: Solve a sale-price break-even that accounts for percentage selling costs
paragraphs: With project cost C, fixed selling cost F and percentage selling fraction s, break-even sale price is (C + F) / (1 − s). The base figures give ($205,000 + $1,500) / 0.94 = $219,680.85. Dividing matters because the selling commission changes with the sale price.

Cash purchase removes the loan’s $8,400 interest and points, raising modeled profit to $36,900 but requiring $196,600 pre-sale cash. It does not make all that cash profit. The familiar 70% ARV heuristic does not itemize these actual assumptions and cannot substitute for a complete budget.
sections.formula: Break-even sale price = (project cost before selling costs + fixed selling costs) / (1 − percentage selling-cost fraction)

sections.title: Reproduce the project and identify excluded risks
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, base pre-selling cost is =150000+4500+35000*(1+10%)+6*600+120000*10%*6/12+120000*2%. Profit is =250000*(1-6%)-1500-project_cost. Cash funding is =project_cost-120000. Keep the sale-price assumption separate from a verified appraisal.

This model uses one fully advanced interest-only acquisition loan capped at purchase price. Renovation and other costs are cash-funded; no staged draws, loan extensions, amortization, contractor sequence, tax deductions or income tax are calculated. Unexpected repairs, legal requirements, sales timing and financing changes still require separate diligence.

flip.chartAlt: Project profit for a base six-month flip, a longer hold, a larger renovation budget, a lower sale price and a cash purchase.
flip.chartCaption: Each scenario changes the stated item from the base. Financing supplies cash and creates interest costs; borrowed principal is not profit.

questions.question: How do I calculate profit on a house flip?
questions.answer: Subtract purchase, closing, renovation including contingency, carrying costs, interest, points and selling costs from the assumed sale price. Keep loan principal financing separate.

questions.question: How much cash do I need before the sale?
questions.answer: In this model, cumulative pre-sale cash funding is project cost before selling costs minus the acquisition loan. It is not just the down payment or a closing-day cash estimate.

questions.question: Does borrowing more create more profit?
questions.answer: No. Loan proceeds are financing and principal is repaid at sale. Interest and points can reduce profit even while borrowing reduces the cash needed before sale.

questions.question: Is the displayed ROI annualized?
questions.answer: No. It is project profit divided by positive pre-sale cash funding. Holding months do not automatically convert that ratio into an annual rate.

questions.question: Does the 70% rule guarantee a profitable purchase?
questions.answer: No. A purchase-price heuristic omits deal-specific costs and cannot verify ARV, repair scope, funding or exit feasibility.

questions.question: Is expected sale price a verified ARV?
questions.answer: No. It is your entered assumption. The calculator does not fetch comparable sales, inspect the property or supply an appraisal.

limitations: One buy-renovate-sell project, before income tax; no recurring rental period or staged construction financing.
All renovation funding is budgeted upfront, with fixed monthly carrying costs and unchanged acquisition principal until sale.
ARV and sale timing are assumptions. No verified profit, safe-offer threshold, market forecast or tax treatment is supplied.

meta.title: How to Calculate PMI and Understand Cancellation Dates
meta.heading: How to Calculate PMI and Understand Cancellation Dates
meta.description: Calculate monthly conventional PMI from a quote and compare the 80% request, scheduled 78% termination and midpoint rules. Includes extra-payment scenarios and scope limits.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate PMI and Understand Cancellation Dates
meta.cardIntro: Calculate monthly conventional PMI from a quote and compare the 80% request, scheduled 78% termination and midpoint rules. Includes extra-payment scenarios and scope limits.

pmi.intro: For a fixed annual borrower-paid PMI quote, monthly premium in this model is original principal multiplied by the annual percentage rate divided by twelve. Estimating the premium is separate from determining when it can stop. Requested cancellation, automatic termination and lender-specific current-value rules are not interchangeable.
pmi.answer: A $400,000 purchase with 10% down has $360,000 original principal. At an entered 0.50% annual PMI quote, initial monthly PMI is $150. For the checked 6.5%, thirty-year fixed loan, the 80% request benchmark is after payment 95, while scheduled 78% is at payment 109. The model assumes an approved request stops premiums at the next payment; the automatic path stops on its scheduled due date if current.

sections.title: Calculate the premium using the quote’s stated basis
paragraphs: The guide uses Use My Quote mode to avoid presenting an illustrative insurer estimate as a current quote. With $360,000 original principal, 0.30%, 0.50% and 0.80% annual quotes give $90, $150 and $240 monthly premiums. The quote model holds that premium basis constant until the selected stopping event or payoff.

PMI is different from homeowners insurance and property tax. The loan-payment figure in this tool excludes those ownership costs. A total mortgage budget needs them separately. The quoted rates are hypothetical inputs; actual insurer premiums and lender billing can vary.
sections.formula: Monthly quoted PMI = original loan principal × annual PMI rate / 100 / 12

sections.title: Use original value for the modeled cancellation benchmarks
paragraphs: For the supported purchase-loan example, original value is the lower of purchase price and appraisal at purchase. A blank purchase-appraisal field assumes it is at least the purchase price. With $400,000 original value, 80% is $320,000 and 78% is $312,000.

A higher current appraisal does not replace that original-value basis in this statutory benchmark model. Investor or servicer current-value cancellation programs can have separate conditions. The existing-loan mode can show current-value LTV for information without treating appreciation alone as an automatic cancellation instruction.

sections.title: The 80% threshold supports a cancellation request, not automatic removal
paragraphs: CFPB’s consumer guidance and its HPA compliance bulletin distinguish the right to request cancellation from automatic termination. The supported request route involves a written request, current payments, good payment history and specified lien and property-value conditions. Reaching the modeled balance threshold is not evidence that these conditions have been established for your actual loan.

Our no-extra-principal case first reaches the 80% benchmark after payment 95. Assuming approval after that payment, the model charges 95 monthly premiums: $14,250 at the 0.50% quote. That payment-count convention is explicit; processing, prepaid premiums, refunds and the insurer contract can change actual costs.

sections.title: Scheduled 78% and final midpoint are separate termination benchmarks
paragraphs: For the supported fixed-rate original schedule, automatic termination generally uses the date principal is scheduled to reach 78% of original value, assuming current payments. It does not substitute the accelerated balance caused by extra principal. The model also checks the month after the original term midpoint and uses the earlier applicable automatic benchmark.

Here scheduled 78% is payment 109, so the automatic-only path contains 108 premium payments, totaling $16,200 at $150 monthly. The thirty-year midpoint benchmark is month 181. The earlier scheduled 78% date controls this example; the guide does not suggest waiting until midpoint when a prior applicable event already ends premiums.

sections.title: Extra principal can advance the request path without moving the original schedule
paragraphs: Adding $500 monthly principal to the same loan advances the modeled 80% request benchmark to payment 44. With request approval assumed, 44 premiums total $6,600. The original scheduled 78% date remains payment 109; the two paths are intentionally separate.

The premium reduction versus the base requested path is $7,650, but the borrower also commits extra principal earlier. Those payments reduce debt and liquidity; they are not a PMI fee or a free return. A full comparison should consider cash availability, interest savings and the servicer’s actual approval conditions.

sections.title: Check which loan and insurance rules actually apply
paragraphs: The model is limited to the stated conventional, borrower-paid monthly PMI setting on an unmodified, fully amortizing fixed-rate principal-residence loan within its disclosed statutory scope. FHA mortgage insurance, VA arrangements, lender-paid insurance, high-risk exceptions and other specialized loan structures are outside it.

In the 20%-down case with original value equal to price, no PMI is modeled. A lower purchase appraisal can change original LTV, so do not turn this example into a blanket promise. For an existing loan, use original loan records, completed-payment count, current principal and the actual servicer premium. Confirm termination with the servicer rather than stopping required payments based on a calculator date.

pmi.chartAlt: Total quoted PMI under assumed approved-request paths at three annual quotes and with extra principal on the same original loan.
pmi.chartCaption: PMI savings are premium differences under the modeled approval convention. Extra principal has its own cash commitment and does not move the original scheduled 78% date.

questions.question: How do I calculate monthly PMI from an annual quote?
questions.answer: In this fixed quote model, monthly PMI = original principal × annual quoted percentage / 100 / 12. A $360,000 principal at 0.50% gives $150 monthly.

questions.question: Does PMI stop automatically at 80% LTV?
questions.answer: No. The supported 80% route is a written cancellation request subject to applicable conditions. The model’s requested-cost path assumes approval; it does not supply it.

questions.question: Do extra payments move the scheduled 78% termination date?
questions.answer: Not in this original fixed-schedule model. They can advance the actual-balance 80% request benchmark, while the original scheduled automatic date remains separate.

questions.question: Can I use a higher current appraisal as original value?
questions.answer: No. Current value can inform a different servicer or investor program, but it does not replace the original-value basis used by these statutory benchmarks.

questions.question: Does this calculate FHA MIP cancellation?
questions.answer: No. FHA and other excluded insurance or loan arrangements have different requirements. Use the relevant program and servicer guidance.

questions.question: Are the quoted annual rates market rates?
questions.answer: No. They are chosen scenario inputs. Use an actual lender or insurer quote for a real comparison and confirm the premium basis and billing convention.

meta.title: How Much House Can I Afford? Income, Debt and Ownership Costs
meta.heading: How Much House Can I Afford? Income, Debt and Ownership Costs
meta.description: Estimate a home price from gross-income ratios or a monthly budget. Compare debt, taxes and HOA costs with five reproducible cases, without treating the estimate as approval.
meta.breadcrumb: How Much House Can I Afford? Income, Debt and Ownership Costs
meta.cardIntro: Estimate a home price from gross-income ratios or a monthly budget. Compare debt, taxes and HOA costs with five reproducible cases, without treating the estimate as approval.

afford.intro: Begin with a housing budget you can sustain, then calculate the loan and home price consistent with that budget and the entered ownership costs. Income ratios are one planning lens; they do not replace take-home cash budgeting or lender review. Existing debts, property tax, insurance, HOA and maintenance can materially reduce the amount left for mortgage principal and interest.
afford.answer: Using $100,000 annual gross household income, $500 monthly other debt and entered 28% housing and 36% total-debt limits, the modeled housing budget is $2,333.33 monthly. With 20% down, a 6% thirty-year loan, 1.2% annual property tax and $1,500 annual insurance, the estimated home price is $380,983.32. These ratios and costs are scenario inputs, not underwriting guarantees.

sections.title: Compare income scenarios without using a salary multiplier
paragraphs: The income comparison above keeps debt, financing and property costs constant. At $60,000 gross annual income, the 36% total-debt ceiling after $500 monthly debt limits housing to $1,300; the modeled home price is $202,711.88. At $80,000 income, the housing budget is $1,866.67 and modeled price is $300,473.64. These estimates also require the displayed down payments; they do not establish that you have enough cash to buy.

At $150,000 income, the same assumptions give a $582,257.53 estimate; at $200,000 they give $783,531.74. These are not recommended purchase prices. A simple income multiplier misses the switch between the housing-ratio and total-debt constraints. Compare actual take-home spending, maintenance, reserves and possible insurance or tax increases before deciding on a budget.

sections.title: Calculate both the housing and total-debt ceilings
paragraphs: Gross monthly income is $100,000 / 12, or $8,333.33 before rounding. At the entered 28% housing ratio, the housing ceiling is $2,333.33. At the entered 36% total-debt ratio, total monthly debt capacity is $3,000. Subtract $500 other monthly debt to leave $2,500 for housing under that second ceiling.

Use the smaller ceiling: $2,333.33. These 28% and 36% values are editable assumptions, not universal lender approval rules. CFPB defines DTI using monthly debt payments and gross monthly income; actual underwriting depends on the loan program, verified income, credit and other conditions.
sections.formula: Housing budget = min(gross monthly income × housing ratio, gross monthly income × total-debt ratio − other monthly debt)

sections.title: Leave room for property costs before sizing the loan
paragraphs: The housing budget must cover more than the loan installment. In the base example, annual property tax is 1.2% of the solved home value and insurance is a fixed $1,500 per year, or $125 monthly. HOA and maintenance are set to zero only to isolate later sensitivities; zero entries are not a claim that a real home needs no maintenance.

The model supports dollar or percentage units. Percentage tax, insurance, HOA or maintenance entries are annual percentages of the solved home value, not percentages of the loan or monthly percentages. Use the selected units consistently. Mortgage insurance is not automatically calculated by this tool; allow for it separately if applicable.

sections.title: Convert the payment budget into an estimated property price
paragraphs: Let a be the monthly payment on one dollar of loan principal at the chosen rate and term. With down fraction d, annual price-linked cost fraction c and fixed monthly costs F, price is (budget − F) / [a × (1 − d) + c / 12]. The price-linked tax assumption means taxes rise as the solved price rises.

For the base inputs, the result is $380,983.32, down payment $76,196.66 and loan $304,786.66. That down payment must be available in cash, with separate funding for closing costs, moving, repairs and reserves. The model does not infer that your savings are sufficient merely because an income-based price can be calculated.
sections.formula: With percentage down payment: price = (housing budget − fixed monthly ownership costs) / [monthly loan-payment factor × (1 − down fraction) + annual price-linked cost fraction / 12]

sections.title: Compare other debt, property tax and HOA on the same income
paragraphs: Increasing other monthly debt to $1,000 leaves only $2,000 under the total-debt ceiling, which now controls. Estimated price falls to $323,476.41 with the other base assumptions unchanged. A debt payment uses monthly capacity even if the borrowed amount itself seems modest.

At the original $500 other debt, raising annual property tax to 2% lowers estimated price to $341,684.84. A separate case adds $300 monthly HOA at the original tax rate and gives $329,227.10. These are controlled sensitivities, not estimated taxes or association charges for a specific home.

sections.title: A fixed monthly budget can be more informative than income ratios
paragraphs: The separate Based on Monthly Budget mode lets you enter a personal housing cap directly. At $2,500 monthly with the base 20% down, rate, term, tax and insurance assumptions, estimated price is $409,736.78. This is a different budget choice, not additional money produced by changing modes.

Compare that entered cap with take-home income after taxes, retirement savings, childcare, transport and other living costs. A lender ratio based on gross income may leave less spending room than a household actually wants. Property expenses can also change over time even when the mortgage note rate is fixed.

sections.title: Reproduce the base estimate and keep its limitations visible
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, budget is =MIN(100000/12*28%,100000/12*36%-500). The monthly loan-payment factor is =-PMT(6%/12,30*12,1). With a 20% down payment and 1.2% annual property tax, price is =(budget-1500/12)/(payment_factor*(1-20%)+1.2%/12). Keep the unrounded intermediate values.

This estimate does not determine a preapproval, rate offer, property valuation, cash-to-close amount or stress-tested personal budget. Use actual tax and insurance information as it becomes available, account separately for mortgage insurance and reserves, and compare loan offers using their complete costs. An estimated maximum is not a recommended purchase target.

afford.chartAlt: Estimated home prices under the same hundred-thousand-dollar gross income with higher other debt, property tax or HOA costs.
afford.chartCaption: Income-ratio cases use entered 28%/36% limits. The table also includes a separate fixed-$2,500 budget case; none are lender approvals.

questions.question: How much house can I afford on a $100,000 salary?
questions.answer: There is no salary-only answer. Under the guide’s specified debt, ratio, rate, down-payment and ownership-cost assumptions, the estimate is $380,983.32. Changing any of those inputs can change the result.

questions.question: Should I enter gross income or take-home pay?
questions.answer: Use gross income in the ratio-based mode, consistent with its DTI construction. Separately check whether the resulting payment fits actual take-home spending and savings needs.

questions.question: Are 28% and 36% required lender limits?
questions.answer: No. They are editable planning assumptions here. Actual underwriting rules, income verification and program requirements can differ.

questions.question: Does the estimate include PMI?
questions.answer: Mortgage insurance is not automatically calculated in this tool. Include an applicable allowance in the budget or other-expense planning and check the dedicated PMI Calculator.

questions.question: Does the down payment cover all cash needed to buy?
questions.answer: No. Closing costs, moving, repairs, reserves and other upfront needs require separate cash planning. This tool does not verify available savings.

questions.question: Is the estimated price a preapproval or recommended maximum?
questions.answer: No. It is a mathematical result under entered assumptions, not a lending decision, appraisal or personal recommendation.

questions.question: How much house can I afford with an $80,000 salary?
questions.answer: Under the income table’s stated assumptions, the estimate is $300,473.64 with $60,094.73 down and a $1,866.67 monthly housing budget. This assumes $500 monthly other debt, 20% down, a hypothetical 6% thirty-year loan, 1.2% annual property tax and $1,500 annual insurance; HOA, maintenance, PMI and closing costs are excluded.

questions.question: How much house can I afford with $20,000 down?
questions.answer: A down payment alone cannot determine an affordable home price. You also need an income or monthly budget, existing debts, loan terms and ownership costs. Select Dollars for the down-payment unit and enter 20000, then account separately for any applicable PMI, closing costs and reserves. This calculator does not automatically calculate PMI or assess loan eligibility.

limitations: Ratios, interest and ownership costs are entered assumptions; no lender program, credit review or income verification is performed.
Mortgage insurance is excluded unless you reserve for it separately. Closing costs and cash reserves are not inferred from the down payment.
Percentage costs use annual fractions of solved home value; future tax, insurance and maintenance increases are not projected here.

meta.title: How to Calculate Personal Loan Payments, Fees and Total Cost
meta.heading: How to Calculate Personal Loan Payments, Fees and Total Cost
meta.description: Calculate personal loan installments, net proceeds and borrowing cost. Compare deducted or financed fees and a longer term using four reproducible examples.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Personal Loan Payments, Fees and Total Cost
meta.cardIntro: Calculate personal loan installments, net proceeds and borrowing cost. Compare deducted or financed fees and a longer term using four reproducible examples.

personal.intro: Start with the repayment balance, interest rate and number of installments. Then reconcile the cash you actually receive with every payment and upfront charge. A payment estimate answers a cash-flow question; it does not establish approval or tell you whether a loan suits your circumstances.
personal.answer: A hypothetical $20,000 personal loan at 12% over 36 monthly payments has a regular installment of $664.29 before insurance. Deducting a 3% origination fee leaves $19,400 net cash while the same installment repays $20,000. Extending that deducted-fee loan to 60 months lowers the installment to $444.89 but increases modeled outflow minus net cash from $4,514.30 to $7,293.34.

sections.title: Calculate the installment from the repayment balance
paragraphs: For the three-year example, the monthly rate is 12% / 12 = 1%, and the number of payments is 36. Apply the amortizing-payment equation to the repayment balance, not automatically to the net cash deposited in your account. The first month’s interest is $200 and the remaining $464.29 of the rounded payment reduces principal.

With no fees or insurance, the unrounded payment stream totals $23,914.30 after final display rounding. Subtract the original $20,000 principal to obtain $3,914.30 modeled interest. The model retains precision internally, so multiplying a displayed payment by 36 can differ from the displayed total.
sections.formula: Payment = balance × monthly rate / [1 − (1 + monthly rate)^(−months)]; at zero rate, payment = balance / months

sections.title: Separate the loan amount, fee and money available
paragraphs: The 3% fee is $20,000 × 3% = $600. With Deducted from proceeds, the repayment balance remains $20,000 and modeled net initial cash is $19,400. Fees do not disappear because they are withheld before the money reaches you. Add documentation and other entered charges before comparing the total.

Paid upfront represents a separate fee payment but uses the same net economic starting cash in this comparison. A bank deposit of $20,000 followed by a separate $600 fee has the same $19,400 net starting position here. Keep the transaction description distinct from the model’s combined net-cash figure.

sections.title: Financing a fee changes what you repay
paragraphs: Choosing Financed adds the $600 fee to the repayment balance, producing a $20,600 balance and $20,000 net initial cash. The installment becomes $684.21. Total installment outflow is $24,631.73, giving $4,631.73 outflow above the cash received under the entered assumptions.

This is not a matched-cash comparison with the deducted-fee example: that case advances only $19,400 net. Decide how much cash the borrowing purpose actually requires, then compare offers that provide that amount. A slightly smaller modeled APR does not by itself identify the better offer when the cash amounts differ.

sections.title: Compare a smaller payment with the full term cost
paragraphs: Keeping the $20,000 balance, 12% rate and deducted fee but extending repayment to 60 months lowers the installment to $444.89. Total installments become $26,693.34. The difference between those payments and $19,400 net cash is $7,293.34, compared with $4,514.30 over 36 months.

The five-year case eases the monthly commitment while keeping the debt outstanding longer. Compare that trade-off with your monthly spending, cash reserve and repayment flexibility. This calculation assumes payments continue as modeled; it does not simulate job loss, missed payments, collections or refinancing.

sections.title: Understand the modeled APR without replacing the disclosure
paragraphs: The model solves a monthly discount rate that equates net cash received with the installment stream including entered insurance, then multiplies that rate by 12. The deducted-fee three-year case gives about 14.1315% nominal cash-flow APR, compared with the entered 12% interest rate. This nominal measure differs from an effective annual compounded yield.

This tool includes all entered insurance in its cash-flow comparison and does not decide which charges belong in a legally disclosed APR. Optional insurance, fee classifications and dated payment rules can change an actual disclosure. Read the lender documents and compare the same measures across offers.

sections.title: Reproduce the payment and choose the right payoff tool
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, =-PMT(12%/12,36,20000) reproduces the base installment. Net proceeds are =20000*(1-3%). For the financed-fee case, replace the repayment balance with 20600 and retain 20000 as net starting cash. Sum the unrounded payment stream before calculating the total cost.

For extra principal on an existing balance, use the linked Loan Repayment Calculator with the actual balance and contractual payment. The Personal Loan form models the contracted schedule and fee-adjusted cash flows; it does not simulate a new extra-payment plan or apply a prepayment penalty. Check contract terms separately.

personal.chartAlt: Modeled personal loan borrowing costs with no fee, deducted fees, financed fees and a longer repayment term.
personal.chartCaption: Fixed monthly hypothetical inputs. Net cash and repayment balances differ between fee treatments; these are not matched-net-proceeds offers.

questions.question: What is the payment on a $20,000 personal loan?
questions.answer: At the stated hypothetical 12% rate over 36 months, it is $664.29 before insurance. The amount changes with the rate, term and financed fees; this is not a current loan offer.

questions.question: Does a longer term save money?
questions.answer: It can reduce the installment while increasing total interest. Compare both the payment and full modeled outflow, keeping cash received and charges visible.

questions.question: Does an origination fee reduce the money I receive?
questions.answer: When deducted, yes. A 3% fee on $20,000 leaves $19,400 net cash in this example; financing instead increases the repayment balance.

questions.question: Is modeled APR the lender’s disclosed APR?
questions.answer: No. This is a cash-flow illustration including entered insurance and fees. It does not classify charges under disclosure rules.

questions.question: Does this check credit or eligibility?
questions.answer: No. Principal, rate and charges are supplied by you. No lender offer or approval is generated.

questions.question: Where can I calculate extra payments?
questions.answer: Use Loan Repayment Calculator for an existing fixed-rate balance. Check prepayment penalties and any excluded charges before interpreting a modeled saving.

limitations: Fixed monthly periods and hypothetical rates; no approval, rate lookup or personalized recommendation.
Keep unrounded calculations until display. Actual contracts may use dated accrual, different fee treatment or payment rounding.
The modeled nominal cash-flow APR includes entered insurance; it does not classify regulatory finance charges or replace a lender disclosure.
No prepayment penalty, variable-rate reset or tax benefit is calculated.

meta.title: How to Calculate Student Loan Payments and Early Payoff
meta.heading: How to Calculate Student Loan Payments and Early Payoff
meta.description: Calculate fixed monthly student loan payments and compare extra principal with a longer term. Four reproducible cases distinguish modeled interest from servicer payoff quotes.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Student Loan Payments and Early Payoff
meta.cardIntro: Calculate fixed monthly student loan payments and compare extra principal with a longer term. Four reproducible cases distinguish modeled interest from servicer payoff quotes.

student.intro: Use the balance entering repayment, an entered fixed rate and the chosen repayment term to estimate a monthly schedule. Then compare extra principal separately from a different contractual term. This guide checks a monthly-period mathematical model, not a federal repayment-plan eligibility calculation or a servicer’s dated payoff quote.
student.answer: For a hypothetical $30,000 balance at 6% over ten years, the modeled payment is $333.06 and total interest is $9,967.38. Adding $100 each month to that contracted payment reduces the modeled payoff to 86 payments and interest to $6,921.10. A twenty-year term instead lowers the payment to $214.93 but increases interest to $21,583.04.

sections.title: Use the repayment balance and distinguish it from original borrowing
paragraphs: The $30,000 case starts with a repayment balance supplied by the user. That amount may differ from the sum of historical disbursements. Check the current statement and separate principal from unpaid accrued interest before applying a model; a single entered balance cannot reproduce the history of multiple loan groups.

This example uses 6% purely as a hypothetical fixed rate. It does not select a federal disbursement-year rate, automatically apply a discount or determine whether interest should be subsidized. For multiple balances with different rates and payment instructions, evaluate the accounts separately rather than treating a simple average rate as an exact replacement.

sections.title: Calculate the fixed monthly payment
paragraphs: Divide the entered annual rate by 12 to obtain 0.5% per month and use 120 monthly periods. The resulting unrounded installment is approximately $333.0615. First-month interest is $150, leaving about $183.06 to reduce principal before display rounding. Later interest falls as the balance decreases.

The model adds each month’s interest to the payment calculation and caps the final installment at the remaining amount due. It retains internal precision instead of rounding every monthly posting to cents. Actual payment dates and servicer rounding can therefore produce a different final figure.
sections.formula: Payment = balance × monthly rate / [1 − (1 + monthly rate)^(−months)]

sections.title: A twenty-year term changes the contract, not just the last payment
paragraphs: At the same $30,000 and 6% but over 240 periods, the modeled installment is $214.93. Total paid is $51,583.04, including $21,583.04 interest. The ten-year case totals $39,967.38, so the smaller twenty-year payment does not imply less total cost.

This is a controlled term comparison, not a claim that a particular federal or private repayment option is available to you. A program may impose additional conditions or use a different payment method. Use current official program resources and the actual lender terms to identify applicable choices.

sections.title: Keep the contractual payment when adding extra principal
paragraphs: In Extra Repayment mode, retain the ten-year term and add $100 monthly. The first payment becomes $433.06 and the schedule ends after 86 payments, with $6,921.10 total interest. The last payment is smaller than the regular combined amount because the model stops at payoff.

With $200 extra monthly, the first payment is $533.06, the schedule takes 67 payments and interest totals $5,317.35. These results assume the extra amount reduces principal after the period’s interest. They do not model a servicer holding cash for a later due date or distributing it among separate loan groups.

sections.title: Monthly model results are different from a dated payoff quote
paragraphs: Daily interest depends on the outstanding balance and elapsed days; this calculator’s examples use equal monthly periods. Edfinancial documents a daily accrual calculation, while CFPB explains payment application and the importance of communicating extra-payment instructions. Neither source endorses these hypothetical rates or example outcomes.

Confirm how your servicer applies extra money and whether it advances the due date. A reduced future bill is not the same modeled action as consistently paying the contractual amount plus extra principal. Obtain an actual payoff amount for a specific date instead of sending the calculator’s remaining principal as a final settlement.

sections.title: Reproduce the example and review excluded decisions
paragraphs: Use =-PMT(6%/12,120,30000) to reproduce the original installment. For each month, calculate interest as opening balance*6%/12 and payment as the smaller of scheduled payment plus extra, or balance plus interest. Subtract principal paid and repeat until the balance is zero.

A decision to prepay can also affect emergency cash, other debt and potential program benefits. This tool does not calculate income-driven payments, forgiveness, tax deductions or the value of federal protections. Do not use the interest difference alone as a recommendation to refinance or abandon a program.

student.chartAlt: Total modeled student loan interest falls with extra monthly principal and rises with a longer contractual term.
student.chartCaption: Same $30,000 balance and 6% entered rate. Extra-payment cases retain the ten-year contractual payment and reduce principal monthly; the final installment is capped.

questions.question: How much is a $30,000 student loan payment?
questions.answer: Under the guide’s hypothetical 6% fixed rate and ten-year monthly schedule, $333.06. A different rate, balance or term changes the result.

questions.question: What does an extra $100 a month do?
questions.answer: In this specific ten-year example, it reduces payoff from 120 to 86 modeled payments and total interest from $9,967.38 to $6,921.10.

questions.question: Does a lower payment mean lower interest?
questions.answer: No. The twenty-year illustration lowers the payment while increasing total interest. Compare both figures under the same balance and rate.

questions.question: Does this calculate income-driven repayment or forgiveness?
questions.answer: No. The examples use fixed monthly amortization. Consult current official resources for program-specific payments and eligibility.

questions.question: Why can my servicer show a different payoff?
questions.answer: Daily accrual, payment dates, unpaid interest, fees, account allocation and rounding can differ from equal monthly periods.

questions.question: Should extra money advance my next due date?
questions.answer: This model assumes principal reduction after monthly interest. Confirm allocation and due-date instructions with the servicer rather than assuming a credit toward future bills has the same effect.

limitations: Fixed monthly periods and hypothetical rates; no approval, rate lookup or personalized recommendation.
Keep unrounded calculations until display. Actual contracts may use dated accrual, different fee treatment or payment rounding.
No income-driven repayment, forgiveness, loan-group allocation or daily payoff quote is calculated.

Edfinancial: daily interest and payment instructions

meta.title: How to Calculate Business Loan Payments and Total Cost
meta.heading: How to Calculate Business Loan Payments and Total Cost
meta.description: Calculate fixed-rate business loan payments, fees and insurance. Compare cash received with full repayment using four reproducible monthly examples.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Business Loan Payments and Total Cost
meta.cardIntro: Calculate fixed-rate business loan payments, fees and insurance. Compare cash received with full repayment using four reproducible monthly examples.

business.intro: Compare the cash a business receives with the full repayment commitment, not just the advertised installment. Fees may reduce working capital at the start, financing fees increases the balance, and separate insurance can add cash outflow outside the principal-and-interest total. The examples below isolate those differences in a fixed monthly model.
business.answer: For a hypothetical $12,000 base loan at 12% over 12 monthly payments, a 3% origination fee plus $120 documentation and $20 other fees totals $500. Deducting those fees leaves $11,500 net cash, with a $1,066.19 monthly installment. Modeled total installment outflow is $12,794.23, or $1,294.23 more than the net initial cash.

sections.title: Begin with net usable cash, not only the headline amount
paragraphs: The base example’s fees are $12,000*3%+$120+$20=$500. Deducted from proceeds leaves $11,500. That difference matters when planning an inventory purchase or project that requires the full $12,000 in cash; the stated principal and usable funding are different quantities.

The modeled starting net cash combines a separate upfront fee with the initial advance when Paid upfront is selected. This common comparison basis does not describe every bank transaction. Review when fees are actually due and whether other charges, deposits or collateral obligations affect available working capital.

sections.title: Match the compounding and payment periods
paragraphs: The checked examples all use monthly compounding and monthly repayments. An entered 12% nominal annual rate becomes 1% per monthly period. Amortizing $12,000 over 12 installments produces $1,066.19 before insurance. Total loan interest is $794.23 and total principal plus interest is $12,794.23.

The calculator also supports other frequency choices, but a nominal rate cannot be compared fairly without its compounding convention. These cases do not demonstrate weekly, daily or revenue-based advances. A factor multiple is not an annual percentage rate and must not be entered as though it were one.
sections.formula: Monthly payment = repayment balance × monthly rate / [1 − (1 + monthly rate)^(−payment count)]

sections.title: Test a longer term against total cash cost
paragraphs: Extending the deducted-fee example to 24 months lowers the modeled payment to $564.88. Total installment outflow rises to $13,557.16, giving $2,057.16 outflow above the $11,500 net initial cash. The same project therefore has a smaller periodic commitment but a larger modeled borrowing cost.

A term comparison is only one part of a cash-flow plan. Revenue can be seasonal and expenses can occur before receivables are collected. The calculator does not assess whether the business can meet each due date, whether collateral is sufficient or whether an entered loan size is appropriate.

sections.title: Financed fees increase the repayment balance
paragraphs: Financing the $500 fees creates a $12,500 repayment balance and $12,000 net starting cash. Payment becomes $1,110.61 over 12 months. Total installments are $13,327.32, or $1,327.32 above cash received. Some of the interest now accrues on financed charges rather than on additional usable cash.

The deducted and financed examples do not advance the same net amount. Compare the funding actually needed before ranking their payments or modeled APRs. Financing may change the timing of a cash burden; it does not erase the charge or establish that an offer is better.

sections.title: Reconcile separate insurance with loan totals
paragraphs: Adding $10 insurance per payment to the original 12-month deducted-fee case increases each full payment to $1,076.19. The engine’s Total payments metric and schedule still report loan principal and interest. Add the separate $120 insurance stream to obtain $12,914.23 overall installment outflow.

The difference between that outflow and $11,500 initial net cash is $1,414.23. The modeled nominal cash-flow APR rises to about 21.9729% because its discount-rate calculation includes that entered insurance. This does not classify regulatory finance charges or guarantee the lender will disclose the same APR.

sections.title: Keep an amortizing term loan separate from SBA or advance pricing
paragraphs: SBA explains that repayment terms vary and distinguishes fixed from variable rates. This generic calculator does not select an SBA program, insert a guarantee fee, apply a program limit or determine eligibility. An applicable fixed-rate quote can be entered manually, but that does not turn the result into an SBA approval estimate.

For the base payment, a spreadsheet can use =-PMT(12%/12,12,12000). For full cash cost, add separate installment charges to loan payments, then subtract net initial cash. Check variable-rate resets, prepayment clauses and other contract charges separately; revenue-based advances require a different model.

business.chartAlt: Modeled business borrowing costs under a longer term, financed fees and per-payment insurance.
business.chartCaption: Fixed monthly hypothetical inputs. Net cash and repayment balances differ between fee treatments; these are not matched-net-proceeds offers.

questions.question: What is the monthly payment on a $12,000 business loan?
questions.answer: At the hypothetical 12% rate over 12 monthly payments, $1,066.19 before insurance. Fees may change net cash or the financed balance.

questions.question: Why do I receive less than the loan amount?
questions.answer: Deducted fees reduce the initial advance. The example’s $500 fees leave $11,500 net from a $12,000 base amount.

questions.question: Does a two-year term cost less than one year?
questions.answer: It lowers the installment in the checked example but increases full modeled outflow above net cash from $1,294.23 to $2,057.16.

questions.question: Does Total payments include separate insurance?
questions.answer: No. Here it covers loan principal and interest. Add insurance per payment times the payment count to reconcile full installment cash outflow.

questions.question: Does this automatically calculate SBA terms?
questions.answer: No. Program fees, eligibility and variable-rate changes are not automatically selected. Use the actual quote and current program information.

questions.question: Can I enter a factor rate as the interest rate?
questions.answer: No. A factor multiple and a nominal annual interest percentage have different meanings. This tool models amortizing borrowing, not percentage-of-sales repayments.

limitations: Fixed monthly periods and hypothetical rates; no approval, rate lookup or personalized recommendation.
Keep unrounded calculations until display. Actual contracts may use dated accrual, different fee treatment or payment rounding.
The modeled nominal cash-flow APR includes entered insurance; it does not classify regulatory finance charges or replace a lender disclosure.
No prepayment penalty, variable-rate reset or tax benefit is calculated.

meta.title: How to Calculate ROI: Profit, Costs and Losses
meta.heading: How to Calculate ROI: Profit, Costs and Losses
meta.description: Calculate investment ROI from profit, initial cost and terminal proceeds. Compare fees, losses, zero recovery and holding periods with six reproducible cases.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate ROI: Profit, Costs and Losses
meta.cardIntro: Calculate investment ROI from profit, initial cost and terminal proceeds. Compare fees, losses, zero recovery and holding periods with six reproducible cases.

roi.intro: Define what went into the investment and what came back before calculating a percentage. ROI measures gain or loss relative to a stated initial cost; it is not the same as revenue, ending value or a compound annual return. Use the same fee and tax basis across comparisons, and keep actual transaction timing visible.
roi.answer: If an investment costs $10,000 and returns $12,000 after one year, its gain is $2,000 and total ROI is 20%. Including a separate $100 entry fee and $100 exit fee changes the modeled initial cost to $10,100 and terminal proceeds to $11,900: gain is $1,800 and ROI is 17.8218%. Fees are included once, rather than ignored or deducted twice.

sections.title: Calculate profit first, then divide by the invested cost
paragraphs: Amount returned is the full terminal value, including any original principal recovered. In the $10,000-to-$12,000 example, the returned amount is $12,000, not just the $2,000 profit. Entering profit in the returned field would instead describe a large loss.

Subtract initial cost from terminal proceeds to obtain the signed dollar gain. Divide that gain by the positive initial cost and multiply by 100. A $2,000 gain on $10,000 is 20%; the same dollar gain on $20,000 is 10%. Neither percentage determines whether the result compensated for risk.
sections.formula: ROI (%) = (terminal proceeds − initial cost) / initial cost × 100

sections.title: Include purchase and sale costs once
paragraphs: The fee-adjusted example adds the purchase fee to initial cash invested and subtracts the sale fee from terminal cash returned. Its gain is $11,900 − $10,100 = $1,800. Dividing by $10,100 gives 17.8218%, rather than the gross example’s 20%. These are explicit hypothetical transaction costs, not a live broker fee schedule.

If a reported ending value or return is already net of a fee, subtracting it again understates the result. Ongoing fees deducted along the way can already be reflected in the ending balance. Investor.gov explains that fees matter; the examples here independently illustrate a single-entry/single-exit convention rather than reconstructing an actual account.

sections.title: Keep negative returns and zero recovery visible
paragraphs: For $10,000 invested and $8,000 returned, the loss is $2,000 and total ROI is −20%. Over two entered years, the compound annual equivalent is approximately −10.5573%. Do not discard the negative sign or describe the remaining $8,000 as a profit.

Zero terminal recovery gives a $10,000 loss and −100% total ROI in the stated unlevered endpoint model. It does not model additional debts or obligations beyond the invested amount. A zero initial cost is different: division by zero has no defined ROI percentage, so the calculator requires positive cost.

sections.title: Separate total ROI from the annualized equivalent
paragraphs: A $10,000 investment returning $15,000 over five years earns 50% total ROI, with an annualized equivalent of approximately 8.4472%. Returning $14,000 over two years earns only 40% total ROI but about 18.3216% annualized. More total dollars and a faster annualized pace answer different questions.

Dividing 50% by five gives an arithmetic 10% per year, not the compound endpoint equivalent. Annualization is a normalization, not evidence that the same outcome can be repeated. The linked annualized-return guide examines period conventions and intermediate cash flows in more detail.
sections.formula: Annualized return (%) = [(terminal proceeds / initial cost)^(1 / years) − 1] × 100

sections.title: Use a different model when money moves during the holding period
paragraphs: This ROI form represents one initial cost and one terminal amount. Contributions, withdrawals, reinvested distributions and operating cash flows at other dates cannot be faithfully summarized by adding every receipt to the ending value and pretending it all arrived at the end.

Use the dated cash-flow tool for actual transaction timing, IRR for appropriately spaced cash flows or Rental Property for a modeled operating and sale sequence. Advertising ROAS compares attributed revenue with ad spend and is not automatically net-profit ROI. This endpoint tool does not fetch market data or choose a good-return threshold.

sections.title: Reproduce the calculation and check its scope
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, =(11900-10100)/10100 produces the fee-adjusted return as a decimal; format the cell as a percentage. For the five-year case, =(15000/10000)^(1/5)-1 gives the compound annual equivalent. Preserve intermediate precision and round only the displayed results.

Use Investment Length for an entered year count. Dates mode uses actual elapsed days divided by 365, so a leap-year interval can differ from one model year. Taxes, inflation, leverage and liquidity need separate consideration; this calculator does not estimate them from the return percentage.

roi.chartAlt: Total ROI and compound annualized return for gross and fee-adjusted gains, a loss, zero recovery and different holding periods.
roi.chartCaption: Single initial cost and terminal proceeds, without intermediate cash flows. Different ending values and holding periods do not compare investment risk.

questions.question: Does amount returned mean profit?
questions.answer: No. It means the full terminal proceeds including any principal recovered. Profit or loss is calculated by subtracting initial cost.

questions.question: How do fees change ROI?
questions.answer: Include entry fees in initial cash invested and reduce terminal proceeds by exit fees, if they are not already included. The stated $100 entry and exit fees reduce the example’s ROI from 20% to 17.8218%.

questions.question: Can ROI be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. Returning $8,000 from a $10,000 initial cost gives −20% total ROI, not a positive 80% return.

questions.question: Is total ROI divided by years the annualized return?
questions.answer: Usually not. The compound annual equivalent uses an exponent, and requires a meaningful holding period and endpoint comparison.

questions.question: Does ROI account for risk or inflation?
questions.answer: No automatic adjustment is made. A return percentage alone does not measure uncertainty, purchasing power or liquidity.

questions.question: What if there are deposits or withdrawals?
questions.answer: Use a cash-flow model that includes their timing. A single-cost/terminal-value comparison can be misleading for transactions during the holding period.

limitations: Hypothetical controlled examples, not forecasts or observed business performance.
No automatic tax, financing, transaction data or personalized recommendation is supplied.
Initial cost must be positive; dates use actual elapsed days divided by 365. Interim transactions require a cash-flow model.

meta.title: How to Calculate Break-Even Point and Target Profit
meta.heading: How to Calculate Break-Even Point and Target Profit
meta.description: Calculate break-even units, sales revenue and target-profit volume. Four reproducible cases show contribution margin, rounding and cost sensitivity.
meta.breadcrumb: How to Calculate Break-Even Point and Target Profit
meta.cardIntro: Calculate break-even units, sales revenue and target-profit volume. Four reproducible cases show contribution margin, rounding and cost sensitivity.

breakeven.intro: Separate fixed costs for one planning period from the variable cost of each unit sold. The difference between unit price and unit variable cost is contribution: the amount available to cover fixed costs before the chosen operating-profit target. This is a volume model, not a prediction of demand or cash availability.
breakeven.answer: With $10,000 fixed costs, a $50 selling price and $30 variable cost per unit, contribution is $20 per unit. Break-even requires 500 units and $25,000 sales revenue. A $5,000 target operating profit raises the required volume to 750 units. If fixed cost instead rises to $10,001, the theoretical requirement is 500.05 units, so whole-unit sales must round up to 501.

sections.title: Match the fixed-cost period to the sales plan
paragraphs: Choose a month, quarter or other consistent period. Fixed costs in this model are the entered costs for that whole period, while variable cost is entered per unit. Combining annual rent with only one month’s sales volume changes the meaning of the result.

Classify costs according to the activity and planning range you are modeling. A cost that looks fixed at one volume can change when capacity expands. This calculator holds its inputs constant; it does not infer whether a particular expense belongs in a fixed or variable category.

sections.title: Calculate the amount each unit contributes
paragraphs: At a $50 price and $30 unit variable cost, contribution is $20. Dividing $20 by $50 gives a 40% contribution margin ratio. It is not net operating margin because fixed costs have not yet been subtracted. Selling price and unit cost must use the same unit definition.

For these quantity modes, price must exceed variable cost. If the contribution is zero or negative, more volume cannot cover positive fixed costs under unchanged assumptions. The calculator rejects such a quantity solution rather than reporting a fabricated break-even sales count.
sections.formula: Unit contribution = unit price − unit variable cost

sections.title: Distinguish theoretical units from whole units sold
paragraphs: The base requirement is $10,000 / $20 = 500 units. Revenue is 500 × $50 = $25,000; variable cost is 500 × $30 = $15,000. Subtracting variable cost and $10,000 fixed cost leaves zero modeled operating profit.

At $10,001 fixed cost, theoretical units are 500.05. Rounding down to 500 leaves a $1 shortfall. Rounding up to 501 produces $25,050 revenue and $19 modeled operating profit. Small positive profit at the displayed whole-unit break-even is therefore expected.
sections.formula: Whole units = ceiling(fixed costs / unit contribution)

sections.title: Add the target profit before solving volume
paragraphs: For a $5,000 target profit, contribution must cover $10,000 fixed costs plus the $5,000 target. At $20 contribution per unit, 750 units are required. Revenue is $37,500; subtract $22,500 variable costs and $10,000 fixed costs to reconcile the $5,000 result.

The target is operating profit under the costs entered. It does not automatically mean after-tax income or cash available for distribution. Interest, tax, financing obligations and any omitted operating costs must be considered separately before interpreting the business result.
sections.formula: Units for target profit = ceiling[(fixed costs + target profit) / unit contribution]

sections.title: Test a higher variable cost and a required selling price
paragraphs: If unit variable cost rises to $35 at the same $50 price, contribution falls to $15. Covering $10,000 fixed costs now needs 666.6667 theoretical units, or 667 whole units. Revenue is $33,350 and the rounded-volume operating profit is $5.

Price mode asks a different question: at 500 entered units, $30 unit variable cost, $10,000 fixed costs and a $5,000 profit target, required price is $30 + $15,000 / 500 = $60. It does not verify that customers will accept this price. Internally calculated prices are not automatically rounded upward to a market quote.

sections.title: Reproduce the result and examine what volume does not prove
paragraphs: In a spreadsheet, =ROUNDUP(10001/(50-30),0) gives the 501-unit case. Profit can be checked with =501*(50-30)-10001. For a target, add it to the fixed-cost numerator before rounding. Keep units and period definitions identical in every comparison.

A break-even count is not a demand forecast, capacity plan or cash-flow schedule. Inventory may require payment before sales arrive, customers may pay later, and multiple products may have different contributions. Use a dedicated sales-mix or working-capital analysis when those details materially affect the decision.

breakeven.chartAlt: Required whole-unit sales volume increases from 500 to 501, 750 or 667 as fixed cost, target profit or variable cost changes.
breakeven.chartCaption: Each case uses a $50 unit price and changes only the stated assumption from the $10,000 fixed-cost / $30 variable-cost base. All costs and targets use the same period.

questions.question: How do I calculate break-even units?
questions.answer: Divide fixed costs by positive unit contribution, then round up if only whole units can be sold. The $10,000 / ($50 − $30) example gives 500 units.

questions.question: Why is profit slightly positive at break-even?
questions.answer: Whole-unit rounding can overshoot the exact fractional requirement. At $10,001 fixed cost, selling 501 units produces $19 modeled profit.

questions.question: How do I calculate sales for a profit target?
questions.answer: Add the target operating profit to fixed costs before dividing by unit contribution. A $5,000 target in the base example requires 750 units.

questions.question: Is contribution margin the same as net margin?
questions.answer: No. Unit contribution is price less variable cost; it must still cover fixed costs before producing operating profit.

questions.question: What if price is no higher than variable cost?
questions.answer: The unchanged model cannot cover positive fixed costs by selling additional units. Quantity modes require positive unit contribution.

questions.question: Does reaching break-even guarantee enough cash?
questions.answer: No. Payment timing, inventory funding, financing and omitted expenses can create cash needs even at the calculated sales volume.

limitations: Hypothetical controlled examples, not forecasts or observed business performance.
No automatic tax, financing, transaction data or personalized recommendation is supplied.
Single-product constant-price model; no sales mix, capacity constraint, working-capital timing or changing variable-cost schedule.
